entry.title: THE MORNING AFTER THE MIRACLES, GREENE COLLECTS FOUR RUNS IN FOUR STRAIGHT VISITS AND CLEVELAND IS WHITEWASHED: TIGERS 6, GUARDIANS 0
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 60 · Sunday, the Sixth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE MORNING AFTER THE MIRACLES, GREENE COLLECTS FOUR RUNS IN FOUR STRAIGHT VISITS AND CLEVELAND IS WHITEWASHED: TIGERS 6, GUARDIANS 0

The very pitching card this paper advertised yesterday — Messick against Valdez — is settled almost single-handedly by Riley Greene: two homers off the young left-hander, a run-scoring single and a run-scoring double besides, four runs driven home in four consecutive turns at bat, no Tiger having done the like since Castellanos in 2017 — and Friday's twice-walk-off heroes are held to three hits entire

Parker Messick tried to finish Riley Greene with a cutter in the first inning Saturday evening, and the pitch arrived over the plate instead of off it. Greene sent it deep to left-center through a crosswind, and the evening at Progressive Field — the bill these pages advertised only yesterday, Messick and his handsome earned-run figure opposing Valdez — had found its author before most of the crowd had found its seats. The man would not be done until he had driven home a run in four consecutive plate appearances: the first-inning blast, a fought-off line single in the third, a second homer leading off the sixth — a 421-foot copy of the first, struck to very nearly the same seat — and a seventh-inning drive off the reliever Festa that screamed for the fence, fell a foot short of a three-homer night, and settled for a run-scoring double. No Tiger had posted runs driven in across four straight visits since Nick Castellanos in the July of 2017. "I was just trying to find barrels, just trying to focus on being on time," Greene shrugged afterward. "The result's the result. They were homers."

The setting made the performance stranger and sweeter both. Greene entered the night a career .168 hitter in Cleveland's yard — nineteen hits in one hundred thirteen regular-season tries — and yet keeps more homers there than in any park save his own; one of them, the scorers note, came off this same Messick in the last days of September a year ago. The two are friendly, All-Star teammates in July, neighbors of a sort in Florida. "I think he owes me a fishing trip that we've been talking about," said the beaten pitcher, who between Greene's blows retired eight straight, five by strikeout, and bore the whole verdict with grace: "He's a great hitter, and he's a huge part of their lineup. I'm sure they're happy to have him back." Detroit's rookie Malgeri added three hits and testified to the phenomenon in plainer words: "He was locked in, and it's contagious." Valdez and the relief corps did the rest — three Cleveland hits all night, not a runner crossing — and Friday's heartbreak of the twice-walked-off doubleheader was answered in the only currency September accepts.

For Cleveland the silence was expensive. Twenty-four hours after Rocchio's two swings wrote the season's gladdest column, the Guardians' hold on the American's last wild-card chair is sole property no longer: Toronto's fourth straight victory, sung in the card below, draws the two clubs level at two-and-seventy wins against one-and-seventy defeats — and the Maple Leaf nine, having taken the season's series four games to two, carry the tiebreaker in their pocket. The Central's account stands unchanged only because Chicago obliged by losing the same evening, that lead holding at two and a half. "Riley had a great game, but our whole team did," said the manager Hinch, declining the singular for the plural as managers must. The desk, unbound by clubhouse etiquette, records what the box score records: one man, four turns, four runs, and a pennant race rearranged by suppertime.

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE GREAT OHTANI SITS A THIRD STRAIGHT NIGHT WITH THE INVALID LIST NOW OPENLY WEIGHED, TROUT'S HAND ESCAPES WITH A BRUISE, AND GRISHAM'S HAMSTRING GIVES WAY AGAIN

The ward's gravest file remains the game's most famous. Shohei Ohtani was held from the Dodger lineup a third consecutive day Saturday — the knee, the biceps, and the neck, the catalogue this ward has carried all week — and the club now weighs the question it has resisted: whether to commit him to the invalid list at all. The rules sharpen the dilemma; a two-way man's minimum stay is fifteen days, as a pitcher's is, and three days is the most any stint may be backdated, so the hour of decision is upon them. "If it doesn't feel good today, then the IL certainly should be on the table," allowed the manager Roberts, who holds out the hope that six or eight days of rest might yet beat fifteen of paperwork. The man himself took his swings in the cage and has not spoken to the press since the seventeenth of August; his club, as the card below attests, keeps winning without him, which settles nothing and soothes everything.

In Pittsburgh the ward held its breath and exhaled. Mike Trout, five-and-thirty now and still the Angels' first citizen, was struck on the left hand by a ninth-inning pitch and left the game; the X-rays came back negative, and the club expects him in the lineup this very afternoon. And in San Diego the Yankees lost the outfielder Trent Grisham to the ten-day invalid list — the right hamstring, the same muscle that shelved him in June, felt first on a stolen-base try Friday night. The club recalled the young Jasson Domínguez from Scranton to fill the post. "It feels like he felt a little bit better today than when he did it a couple of months ago," offered the manager Boone, hopefully. Swift knitting to every name above, and to the great one especially.

THE MILESTONE DESK: MURAKAMI MAKES IT THREE SOUTH SIDERS AT THIRTY HOMERS APIECE — AND THE CROWNS OF BOTH LEAGUES' FENCE-CLEARERS TIGHTEN BY A SWING

The trio this desk half-promised on Friday is complete. Munetaka Murakami, the left-handed slugger crossed over from Japan this winter past, opened Saturday's contest with a towering two-run blast to left — his thirtieth of the season, and the blow that makes the White Sox a club with three thirty-homer men, Vargas and Colson Montgomery having reached the figure together only the night before, as these pages sang yesterday morning. It is but the fourth such season in the franchise's long annals, the company being the vintages of 2004, 2006, and 2008. Murakami joins Ohtani, Suzuki, and the great Matsui as the only Japanese-born men ever to strike thirty in an American season — and Montgomery, two batters later, answered with his one-and-thirtieth to reclaim the club lead, the tenth time the two have homered in the same game this year. That the evening ended in defeat, the card below relates; the slugger declined all consolation: "Obviously I'm really happy about getting 30, but moreover we lost the game. So that's very much disappointing."

The desk lifts its eyes to the leagues' twin crowns while it is about the arithmetic. In the American, Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero struck his eight-and-thirtieth Saturday in Arlington to pad his lead over Houston's Alvarez at seven-and-thirty, with New York's Rice at six-and-thirty close astern. In the National, Philadelphia's Kyle Schwarber answered Acuña's theatrics with his one-and-fortieth, while Chicago's Crow-Armstrong — whose pursuit of forty this desk has followed all week — went homerless in Miami and stands yet at nine-and-thirty, the threshold still one swing distant. One-and-twenty days remain; the desk commends both tables to the reader's morning attention.

THE RESTORATION DESK: THE CAPTAIN STANDS AT THE FINISH LINE, THE WIRES COUNT EIGHT CAVALRIES COMING, AND EVERY CONTENDER CHECKS ITS CALENDAR

The wire desks Saturday drew up a muster roll of the wounded who may yet rejoin the season's last battles, and the first name upon it is the one these pages have tracked since May. Aaron Judge, absent from the Yankee lineup since the one-and-thirtieth of that month with the fractured rib, took batting practice on the Petco field a second straight day and is expected to stand in against live pitching Monday; the hope, openly held, is a return during the homestand New York opens Tuesday against Colorado. "He's at the finish line to be ready to play," said the manager Boone Saturday night, and the clubhouse speaks of it like men awaiting a ship. "We're all as eager to have him back now as we were right when he went out," said Rice.

The rest of the roll reads like reinforcements posted to every front of the wild-card wars. Boston's Garrett Crochet, runner-up for last year's American pitching laurels, threw off a mound Friday for the first time in more than three months and may return this month as a relief weapon. Arizona's Corbin Burnes, lost to the surgeon's table eleven starts into his desert tenure, has begun rehabilitation starts and could rejoin a club presently seated in the National's last chair; San Diego's Nick Pivetta, shelved since April, progresses toward a return within days for the very club chasing that chair. And in Houston, Carlos Correa — whose 2026 seemed finished upon the ankle surgeon's May verdict — runs at nearly full speed and shifts his rehabilitation to the club's Florida grounds, an improbable October card not yet ruled out. The desk notes the pattern with approval: September's scrums shall be settled not only by who is standing, but by who gets back up.

THE MATTER OF THE TILTED CAP, CONCLUDED: AN UMPIRE'S APOLOGY ON THE FIELD, A CLUBHOUSE IN CROOKED BRIMS, AND THE ACCUSED CATCHER CLEARS HIS NAME

The Herald confesses a weakness for a story in which the pastime remembers its manners, and Denver supplied one Saturday. The reader will want the Friday prologue: in the sixth inning of his major-league debut, the Cardinal rookie Hancel Rincon was directed by the umpire Eddings to straighten the angle of his cap's bill — no rule forbidding it, the arbiter later conceded, only an "unwritten" one — and the argument that followed cost the manager Marmol his evening. Saturday the game answered in kind. Cardinal players, coaches, and their faithful alike wore their own brims at a defiant tilt in solidarity with the young man; Eddings stopped Rincon on his walk to the bullpen and, by the pitcher's account, apologized and wished him luck in his career. "I told him, 'Don't worry, it's nothing personal, and everything stays here,'" said Rincon, who then threw a spotless sixth inning and banked the first strikeout of his major-league life. "I felt big support from my teammates. Obviously, when you are together, like this group, we're gonna be much better."

There remained only the matter of the man wrongly named. The wires had identified Colorado's catcher Hunter Goodman as the complainant whose word set the whole affair in motion, and Goodman — stung by two days of anonymous abuse over it — flatly denied the charge Saturday: "I never once mentioned the hat. I don't care how they wear the hat. I'm trying to find out where the ball is coming out." His own manager pressed Eddings on the point and reports the umpire never named Goodman at all. The catcher then went out and struck the bases-loaded single that decided the actual ballgame, as the card below relates — proof, if the desk may editorialize, that the surest answer to a controversy remains a base hit. The Herald tips its cap to all parties. At a slight angle.

The Rest of the Card

ABOVE THE WATERLINE AT LAST — OKAMOTO'S FOUR HITS CARRY TORONTO LEVEL WITH CLEVELAND, TIEBREAKER IN POCKET: MAPLE LEAF NINE 4, ROYALS 3

For the first time since the third of April, the Blue Jays' wins outnumber their defeats — two-and-seventy against one-and-seventy — and the club celebrated the crossing by seizing a share of the American's last wild-card chair, the head-to-head verdict over Cleveland already banked as this paper recorded on Friday. The evening's engine was Kazuma Okamoto, whose first four-hit night in the majors ran to two doubles, a rare single driven the opposite way, and two runs cashed; the ancient Max Scherzer, two-and-forty years old and mending all season, gave five and two-thirds of three-run ball and pronounced himself stronger by the outing: "I feel healthy, I feel good, everything's in a good spot." Toronto struck first with two in the opening frame, absorbed Kansas City's answer, and went ahead for keeps in the seventh, Fluharty winning in relief of the veteran with Varland sealing his three-and-thirtieth save; the loss fell to Kimbrel. "We struck first, got punched back in the mouth and stayed on it," ruled the manager Schneider, whose club has won four running and eight of ten — the hottest hand in the entire scrum — and goes for the sweep at 2:10 this afternoon.

NINE DAYS' REST, SEVEN SPOTLESS INNINGS, AND A SECOND STRAIGHT WHITEWASHING AT THE HARBOR: FENWAY MEN 5, BALTIMORES 0

The winningest arm in the American took the hill precisely as yesterday's desk note advertised, and pitched like a man who had spent his nine days' holiday sharpening knives. Sonny Gray, six-and-thirty and deliberately rested since the six-and-twentieth of August, carried seven scoreless innings of three hits for his seventeenth victory against four defeats — Boston's second consecutive shutout of the Orioles, a first for the club this season — and admitted afterward that Friday's benches-clearing theatrics had seasoned his purpose: "We wanted to kind of bury these guys, especially after whatever that dude was trying to do last night." The scoring was patient work: Eli White's two-out, bases-loaded dunker cashed two in the sixth, Wong cashing a third behind him, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa — lately returned from the ward himself — doubled home two in the seventh before saving the eighth with a diving stop, that inning's true crisis passing when Weissert struck out Alonso with the bases full. Baltimore has now lost five running, stands three from the last chair, and sends its faithful to a 1:35 finale hoping to avoid the broom; Boston, winners of three straight, sits six clear in the wild-card row's second seat.

THE FREE PASS TO THE MAN AHEAD IS TAKEN AS AN INSULT AND ANSWERED WITH THREE RUNS: TAMPA MEN 6, LONE STAR NINE 3, IN TEN INNINGS

Arlington's tenth-inning arithmetic was orthodox — the automatic runner bunted along, first base open, an intentional pass to the dangerous Díaz — and Jonathan Aranda, standing on deck through all of it, read the strategy as an affront: "When they intentionally walked him, I took it personally." He drove Latz's 1-2 slider 409 feet to right-center with two aboard, and the verdict was written. The blast decorated a night of superior pitching: Drew Rasmussen gave seven innings of one run and three hits without a walk, outlasting the great deGrom pitch for pitch, his only blemish Pederson's first-pitch homer in the sixth; Junior Caminero supplied his eight-and-thirtieth homer, the American's leading count, and Palacios his eighth, with Wells — the deadline acquisition from Baltimore, of all provisioners — throwing two scoreless frames for the win. Texas banked two in the eighth to force the extra chapter and no more; the Rangers have dropped two running and slip two full games from the last chair, while the Tampa men hold the East by four with the clubs meeting again at 2:35 this afternoon.

RICE REACHES IN ALL FIVE VISITS, RODÓN PERMITS TWO HITS, AND A FOUR-AND-THIRTIETH LEVEL SEASON IS BANKED: BRONX BOMBERS 5, SAN DIEGO NINE 1

The Yankees' one-and-eightieth victory carried a quiet civic guarantee — a four-and-thirtieth consecutive season no worse than level, a run of institutional stubbornness dating to 1993 — and was built on the era's least Yankee-like virtues: patience and the single. Ben Rice reached base in all five plate appearances, three singles and two walks, sprayed with such line-to-line craft that his manager reached for the highest local compliment: "I told him, he's doing his Tony Gwynn imitation." The second inning did the heavy work — three consecutive walks, Goldschmidt's forcing in a run, Cody Bellinger's two-run single behind them — and Ray was gone after seven outs, charged with five. Carlos Rodón made it stand with five innings of two hits and seven strikeouts, Machado's five-and-twentieth homer the only Friar coin, and the local boy Spencer Jones added two more hits to his homecoming week. The freight ran south as well as north: San Diego's defeat, paired with Arizona's ten-inning heroics below, surrenders the National's last chair by half a game — and the same clubs close the set at 4:10 this afternoon, Cole opposing King.

FOUR RELIEVERS THROW THE SILENCE, MARTE LEVELS IT, AND THE LAST CHAIR CROSSES THE DESERT ONCE MORE: SNAKES 4, ASTROS 3, IN TEN INNINGS

The chair this paper has watched change hands all week changed hands again by the Houston midnight — the fifth transfer inside seven mornings — and Arizona took it back with its bullpen's finest hour. Down 3-1 behind Pfaadt's honest six and a third, the Snakes chipped to within one in the seventh, drew level on Ketel Marte's eighth-inning homer to right, his two-and-twentieth, went ahead in the tenth, and then asked the young Brandyn Garcia to hold it against the heart of the order: he struck out the mighty Alvarez looking on a 98-mile sinker to open the frame and ended the night fanning Altuve on one harder still. "I did try to let that one eat as hard as I could," the closer grinned, his fifth save banked behind Loáisiga's win. Four relievers — Ginkel, Morillo, Loáisiga, and Garcia — covered three and two-thirds without a run, Morillo's scoreless string reaching eighteen games; the manager Lovullo's verdict, "that's the reason why we win so many one-run games here," reads like the season's thesis. Houston's lead in the West holds at three over beaten Texas, but the second seed stays a game and a half distant — and the clubs go again at 2:10, Arizona sending Rodriguez and his fourteen victories to press the advantage.

THE MILESTONE EVENING GOES FOR NAUGHT — JEFFERS' THREE-RUN BLOW OVERTURNS THE TRIO'S THUNDER: TWIN CITIES NINE 6, SOUTH SIDERS 4

Chicago's first inning made franchise history, as the milestone desk above relates at proper length — Murakami's two-run thirtieth, Montgomery's one-and-thirtieth two batters later, three runs and three thirty-homer men on one September scorecard — and Minnesota spent the middle innings dismantling the celebration. Two runs in the fourth drew close, and in the fifth Ryan Jeffers turned on Kay for a three-run blast, his fourteenth, that stood the ledger on its head; a seventh-inning run supplied the margin, and Bradley — the very arm that had surrendered the milestone — settled in for his eleventh victory, Gómez sealing the one-and-twentieth save. The South Siders' lead in the Central holds at two and a half over Cleveland — beaten the same evening, as the lead column relates — and their game-and-a-half hold on the American's second seed survived the night besides, Houston having lost in sympathy. The clubs conclude their season's business at 6:20 this evening, Ober opposing Hudson, and the White Sox will be glad to see the back of a Minnesota club that keeps spoiling their parties.

SPRINGS SCATTERS THE SOUND'S BATS AND THE SPOILERS RUN THEIR STRING TO FOUR: MACKMEN 6, MARINERS 2

The Athletics continue their September office with the relish of men who have nothing to lose and lately lose nothing: a fourth consecutive victory, built early and defended late. Lawrence Butler's thirteenth homer and Max Muncy's ninth — the Athletics' own Muncy, the desk hastens to note, no relation to the Angeleno — carried a lead that grew by installments through four innings, Bolte and Walton doubling home the trimmings, and Jeffrey Springs made it stand for his fourth victory, the Mariners held to six hits and their two runs arriving only after the issue was settled, Kirby bearing the loss. Seattle has now dropped three running and eight of its last ten, a once-plausible September now visible chiefly in the rearview; the Mackmen, last in the West and first in mischief, get their chance at a sweep at 4:10 this afternoon.

KIKUCHI'S FIRST VICTORY OF THE YEAR ARRIVES IN SEPTEMBER, AND TROUT LEAVES WITH A BRUISE, NOT A BREAK: HALOS 6, CORSAIRS 1

The Angels' second win in their last twelve engagements was a night of small mercies. Yusei Kikuchi, winless through five defeats this season, carried the decision at last behind twelve hits of support — Meckler doubling twice, Nathaniel Lowe homering, Trout and Neto cashing runs — while Pittsburgh's Bryan Reynolds supplied the home nine's whole account with his sixteenth homer, the loss falling hard on Ashcraft and his fourteen victories. The anxious moment came in the ninth, when Mike Trout took a pitch off the left hand and departed; the X-rays read clean, as the ward above records with relief, and the great man is expected back for the rubber match. That engagement carries the day's most interesting name: Paul Skenes takes the hill for the Corsairs at 1:35 against Ureña and his 2.85 — the sort of Sunday bill that makes a last-place visitor's trip worthwhile.

ACUÑA ADMIRES HIS THUNDER AT LEISURE, AND WHEELER RENDERS THE FULL-COUNT JUDGMENT: PHILLIES 4, ATLANTAS 2

The night's theatre was a duel inside the duel. Ronald Acuña Jr. struck a 450-foot blast off Zack Wheeler in the third and toured the bases at a promenade, savoring every boo Citizens Bank Park could raise; Kyle Schwarber answered an inning later with his one-and-fortieth homer, the majors' leading count, and Wheeler filed the insult for the fifth, when he ran Acuña to a full count and blew a 96-mile fastball past him on the outside corner to strike out the side. "Our guy just rounds the bases — who hits 50 here," the pitcher observed afterward, the jab aimed with the same precision as the fastball. "I really wanted to strike him out right there and kind of get him back." Wheeler's whole line — six innings, three hits, nine strikeouts, nineteen swings-and-misses, one run — reads like a man emerged from his August troubles; Riley's sixteenth homer trimmed the margin in the seventh before Duran sealed his thirtieth save. The East's lead is cut to four games, the Phillies sit half a game behind Chicago for the wild card's first chair, and the set concludes at 1:10 this afternoon, Mahle opposing Nola.

THE BOBBLEHEAD WORKS ITS ANNUAL MAGIC — DE LA CRUZ'S EFFIGY-DAY BLAST HELPS FELL THE GAME'S BEST LEDGER: REDS 5, BREWERS 3

The Queen City has learned to schedule its miracles: for the second consecutive season, Elly De La Cruz homered on the night the club handed out his likeness in miniature, crushing May's 0-2 fastball a tracked 438 feet to the berm beyond center — his two-and-twentieth, his first since the two-and-twentieth of August, and the levelling blow in an evening Cincinnati won by degrees. Stephenson and McLain added fifteenth homers apiece, Santillan took the decision, and Pagán sealed the one-and-twentieth save while Milwaukee's Ashby — a man beaten only twice all season entering — absorbed his third defeat, Contreras's fourteenth homer the visitors' best answer. The Brewers' lead in the Central slips to seven over surging Chicago, the first time in weeks the gap has worn single digits so thin; the clubs go directly again at 12:10 this very noon, Harrison opposing Singer, the day's earliest bell.

THE TWO-HUNDREDTH BALL LEAVES A YARD WHERE BALLS SELDOM LEAVE, AND A NEW MAN SURVIVES THE NINTH: CUBS 6, MIAMI NINE 5

Chicago's evening in Miami banked two firsts: Michael Conforto's third-inning drive, 411 feet to center in a park that discourages the practice, was the club's two-hundredth homer of the season — no other club in the majors has yet reached the figure — and the ninth belonged to Ryan Zeferjahn, who recorded five outs for his first save in Cub flannels, pacing the dugout between innings to keep his blood warm. "I got the best defense behind me, and I let them work, and it came up huge," said the reliever, whose 7.20 figure after the deadline trade had tried the faithful's patience. The offense gathered six runs by the sixth — Happ driving in two, Crow-Armstrong, Busch, and Hoerner a run apiece — and then held its breath as Miami closed to one; Rolison improved to eight victories against a single defeat. The forty-homer question stands unanswered another morning, the center fielder held in the yard at nine-and-thirty, and the Cubs — winners of three straight, half a game up on Philadelphia for the wild card's first chair — send Holmes and his 2.09 against Phillips at 1:40 to close the set.

SIX BALLS LEAVE CITI FIELD IN GIANT LIVERY — TWO FROM DEVERS, TWO FROM THE UNHERALDED KOSS: ORANGE AND BLACK 9, FLUSHING NINE 5

Rafael Devers is conducting one of the hot streaks the annals keep: two more homers Saturday — the five-and-thirtieth among them — run his six-game account to six homers and seven walks, a combination no Giant has managed since 1900 save Barry Bonds in 2004 and Willie Mays in 1958. Yet the day's charm belonged to Christian Koss, owner of one homer in 138 tries entering, who struck two — his first multi-homer game at any level since a High-A afternoon in 2021 — and confessed the simplest philosophy in the game: "Hit the ball hard and hope good things happen." Basabe and McCray joined the parade for six balls over the Flushing fences in all, Molina winning his third as a Giant, and the evening even supplied farce: the manager Vitello was ejected in the second inning for emerging to discuss a foul-ball challenge — "I walked out without any fire in me," the puzzled skipper testified, "and I got thrown out for walking out of the dugout." Ewing's two-run homer led the Mets' portion. The clubs settle the set at 1:40 this afternoon, Perdomo opposing Scott.

HITLESS THROUGH FOUR, SIX RUNS IN THE FIFTH — THE MILE HIGH NINE OVERTURN THE EVENING ENTIRE: MILE HIGH NINE 10, CARDS 7

St. Louis had built the game these pages expected: a 3-0 lead on Joshua Báez's second-inning homer and Iván Herrera's two-run fifth-inning blast — that man's second of the series, his ninth-inning thunder having decided Friday's contest in these very columns — while Liberatore retired ten straight and carried a no-hit account into the fifth. Whereupon Coors Field did what Coors Field does: six runs in the frame, six hits and two wild pitches and an error among them, and a four-run seventh behind it, sparked by Hunter Goodman's bases-loaded single — the same catcher whose name the cap affair had dragged through two days' mud, as the news columns above relate, answering his critics in the game's oldest language. "It keeps happening in slightly different ways, which makes it incredibly frustrating," said Liberatore of the recurring fifth-inning ambush that now marks his 5-14 ledger; Bernardino took the win, Romano the fifteenth save, and the rookie Rincon, crooked cap and clear conscience, threw his spotless sixth. The Cards slip a game under level and four from the last chair; the set is decided at 3:10 this afternoon.

THE STAND-IN AT THE TOP OF THE ORDER ROBS WITH THE GLOVE AND DECIDES WITH THE BAT: BOYS IN BLUE 6, SENATORS 5

Three nights into the great Ohtani's absence, the leadoff post belongs to Tommy Edman, and the utility man is keeping it warm to the point of scorching. In the fifth he went full-stretch at the left-center wall to take extra bases — his pitcher thought a homer — away from Lile; in the seventh, with the champions down 4-2 and two aboard, he turned on Beeter's slider and drove it deep to right for the go-ahead three-run blast, his sixth of the year. "When you don't have Shohei in there, to put Tommy in there and really still be productive, it's great," said the manager Roberts, whose lineup card had also lost Muncy to illness and Rushing to a sore elbow two hours before the bell. Glasnow ground through six-plus without his best stuff, Washington's Daylen Lile drove in two, and the capital club's ninth-inning run made Scott's one-and-twentieth save honest work, Vesia taking the decision. The champions have won three running, hold the West by ten and a half, and go for the sweep at 10:10 tonight — the card's lone lamplighter's shift, Wrobleski and his eleven victories against Alvarez.

The tables this Sunday morning read thus. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the East by four over New York, Boston seven and a half astern; the White Sox keep the Central by two and a half over Cleveland, their second-seed cushion a game and a half over Houston; the Astros hold the West by three over Texas. The wild-card row is the morning's theatre: New York and Boston secure, and the last chair now a bench for two — Toronto and Cleveland level at two-and-seventy wins apiece, the Maple Leaf nine holding the season-series tiebreaker, with Texas two behind and Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta by four over Philadelphia; Milwaukee by seven over Chicago; Los Angeles by ten and a half over Arizona — and the wild-card ledger reads Chicago's first chair by half a game over the Phillies, with the last chair returned to Arizona by half a game over San Diego, Miami and St. Louis four back. Today's bill is a Sunday feast of fifteen engagements, nearly all of them by daylight and all verified against the schedule; the desk directs the eye to five. At 12:10 in Cincinnati the Brewers seek their remedy at once, Harrison opposing Singer; at 1:10 in Philadelphia the East's argument concludes, Mahle against Nola; at 1:35 in Pittsburgh the Corsairs send Skenes against Ureña and his 2.85; at 1:40 in Cleveland the whitewashed Guardians hand the ball to Williams and his thirteen victories against the rookie Jobe, with a chair to defend; and at 2:10 in Houston Arizona presses its reclaimed advantage behind Rodriguez, he of the fourteen victories and the 2.59. The late shift is short and sweet: New York at San Diego at 4:10, Cole opposing King, and the night owls' lone reward at 10:10, the champions going for the sweep at Chavez Ravine. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: A GRAND SLAM TO COME LEVEL AND A WALK-OFF BLAST TO END IT — ROCCHIO JOINS A LIST FIVE NAMES LONG SINCE 1924: GUARDIANS 7, TIGERS 6
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 59 · Saturday, the Fifth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 16 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

A GRAND SLAM TO COME LEVEL AND A WALK-OFF BLAST TO END IT — ROCCHIO JOINS A LIST FIVE NAMES LONG SINCE 1924: GUARDIANS 7, TIGERS 6

Down six runs to one by the third inning of a doubleheader's opening chapter, Cleveland is restored by one man's two swings: Brayan Rocchio's first career grand slam levels the account in the fourth, his first-pitch blast over the nineteen-foot wall in the ninth ends it — five runs driven in, a page in the Elias ledger beside Greenberg and Miñoso, and the nightcap, as the card below sings, obliged with a second walk-off besides

The gentlemen of the Elias Bureau keep a very short list: men who struck a grand slam and a walk-off homer in the selfsame game. When Friday began it read five names, and the freshest of them was five-and-thirty years old — George Kelly of the 1924 Giants, Hank Greenberg of 1938, Minnie Miñoso of 1960, Otto Velez of 1980, Jack Clark of 1991. By Friday evening at Progressive Field it read six, and the sixth was Brayan Rocchio, shortstop of the Guardians, a man batting .177 since the All-Star interval and lately so far gone in frustration that he hurled his bat to the earth Thursday and wanted the counsel of two veterans to gather himself. "I told them, 'Bro, I feel so comfortable at the plate. But I don't have the results,'" Rocchio confessed of that conversation with Hedges and Lowe. Friday, the results arrived all at once.

The day had opened as badly as a September day can. Detroit battered the starter Allen for four first-inning runs — two-run singles from the rookie Malgeri and the young Max Clark — added a fifth on a double play, and a sixth on Spencer Torkelson's two-and-twentieth homer: six runs to one before the third inning was cold. The home fourth answered in two strokes: Travis Bazzana's run-scoring single, and then, with the bases full, Rocchio turning on a hung curveball from Montero and depositing it over the right-field wall — the first grand slam of his major-league life, in the first two-homer game of it, the account level at six. Four relievers — Cecconi, Yoho, Sabrowski, and Smith — held the line from there, and in the ninth Rocchio stood in against the left-hander Sommers and wasted not a single pitch: the first offering, a four-seamer, sent 405 feet over the nineteen-foot wall in left. Bedlam, a bat flung skyward, and a 7-6 verdict — struck, the scorers noted, from both sides of the plate, the twentieth such game in the club's annals and the first since José Ramírez in 2023.

The faithful of northeast Ohio have a name for this seasonal phenomenon — "Playoff Rocchio," earned by a .375 division series in 2024 and a walk-off three-run blow in last year's finale — and his manager Vogt asked only that the moment be enjoyed: "What a cool day for him today. That was really fun." The reliever Sabrowski put the clubhouse's faith plainer still: "When it's a clutch situation and he's up, we believe it's going to happen." The arithmetic was not done with the day, for a second game waited and delivered a second walk-off, as the card below relates; taken together the two verdicts keep Cleveland's last wild-card chair from a gathering crowd — the Canadians now a single game astern, Texas two, Baltimore three — with the Central's leaders but two and a half ahead. The desk merely observes that the season's great virtue is its patience: it waited until September to hand a struggling man the finest day of his baseball life.

News Around the League

THE VESTIBULE OF SPRING: THE 2027 EXHIBITION CALENDAR IS PUBLISHED — ALL THIRTY CLUBS TO OPEN ON THE NINETEENTH OF FEBRUARY, ONE HUNDRED SEVEN-AND-SIXTY MORNINGS FROM THIS ONE

The league on Friday published the whole of the 2027 spring exhibition schedule, and this paper — whose masthead exists to ask a single question of the calendar — records the answer with particular satisfaction: for the first time under the new arrangement, all thirty clubs of the Cactus and Grapefruit Leagues open on the same day, the nineteenth of February. The opening bill includes the Dodgers and White Sox at their shared Camelback Ranch grounds in Glendale and the Yankees calling at Dunedin to try the Blue Jays; the spring's closing ornaments include the Freeway Series between the Los Angeles clubs from the one-and-twentieth of March to the three-and-twentieth, and Tampa Bay receiving Toronto at Tropicana Field on the twentieth. The regular campaign follows at once: an Opening Night engagement on the four-and-twentieth of March — a date the schedule-keepers at Baseball-Reference confirm — with the traditional Opening Day of fourteen games the day after.

The desk performs the arithmetic its readers expect of it: one hundred seven-and-sixty mornings separate this edition from the first spring pitch. It is a comfort peculiar to September that even as the present season sharpens toward its last three weeks, the next one has already posted its address.

THE RESTORATION DESK: THE CAPTAIN TAKES HIS SWINGS AT LAST — JUDGE SPRAYS LINE DRIVES AT PETCO AND EYES THE HOMESTAND

The return these pages have watched hovering since midsummer drew visibly nearer Friday afternoon in San Diego, where Aaron Judge stepped into the cage on a big-league field for the first time since the one-and-thirtieth of May and sprayed line drives about the Petco outfield. The captain of the Yankees, mending from the fractured right rib he sustained in late April, called the session "checking another box"; he ran the bases besides, took fly balls in right field, and delivered a one-hop throw to third from medium depth. "I'm mad how long it has taken," the man admitted. "We're getting close. I can't wait to be back out there." What remains is live pitching — "a couple of times, at least," by his own reckoning — and the question of whether a minor-league errand precedes the return; Judge would prefer to skip it, and his manager Boone has decided nothing. The hope, by the wires' account, is the homestand the Yankees open against Colorado on the eighth, and the paper notes one date the club has already circled: the eleventh of September, when the Mets visit and, as the team announced Friday, alumni of the 2001 Yankees gather for the pregame ceremonies. "If I'm playing or not playing, it's going to be special," said Judge. The ward, for its part, would simply like its most famous patient discharged.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: TAMPA'S ACE RETURNS TO THE INVALID LIST, CLEVELAND'S SWEEP EXACTS ITS TOLL, AND A BLUE JAY LEAVES AFTER TWO INNINGS

The ward's heaviest entry is Tampa Bay's: Shane McClanahan, beaten in Arlington Thursday as yesterday's card recorded, reported tightness in the left forearm after his fifth inning there and was dispatched Friday to the fifteen-day invalid list — his second visit of the season, for a man only this year returned from two lost seasons and the surgeon's table. "Anytime a guy talks about his arm, we're going to do right by him," said the manager Cash, while the pitcher himself counseled calm: the club moved quickly, he said, "to not let this compound, not let this snowball." His ledger stands at 3.36 across 118 innings; the American's best record can absorb the absence, but October arithmetic is another matter.

Cleveland's glorious Friday, the lead column notwithstanding, sent two men to the ward's counter: Chase DeLauter left the nightcap with a sprained right wrist and is called day-to-day, and Angel Martínez departed the same game with a shoulder contusion after colliding with Rocchio in the outfield — precautionary, the club says, and the ward chooses to believe it. In Kansas City, Toronto's Jameson Taillon, activated that very day from the forearm trouble that shelved him, lasted two innings before right elbow discomfort ended his evening — the sort of sentence a training staff reads twice. The Yankees' Trent Grisham left San Diego with a balky right hamstring; and in Los Angeles the great Ohtani sat out a second consecutive game, the knee-biceps-neck catalogue this ward has tracked all week still under management. Swift knitting to every name above.

THE VALEDICTORY DESK: DETROIT APPOINTS TWO DAYS FOR VERLANDER'S FAREWELL, AND THE OLD LION WANTS ONE MORE TURN ON THE HILL

The Tigers have fixed the ceremonies: the five-and-twentieth and six-and-twentieth of September, the final home weekend, two days given over to Justin Verlander — a pregame tribute with speakers and gifts on the Friday, a charitable endowment in his name on the Saturday, bobbleheads for the first fifteen thousand through the gates, and the faithful encouraged to wear orange, that being the one color all four of his employers — Tigers, Astros, Mets, and Giants — have flown. What remains unfixed is the part the man himself cares most about: whether he pitches again before the curtain. A hamstring has set him back by weeks at a stretch, and at each setback the calendar has shortened. "I'm not giving up, but trying to be as smart as I can about not having a setback," Verlander said Friday, reporting a bullpen session near and his velocity lately "really healthy." He is equally plain about his terms: he will not take the hill hurt, and he will not take it as theatre — "I'm not trying to go out there and make a fool of myself. But if I'm healthy enough, then I don't see why I can't." The Herald, which has set down twenty years of the man's deeds, hopes the last entry is written on the mound and not merely beside it.

THE MILESTONE DESK: THIRTY AND THIRTY ON THE SAME EVENING — VARGAS AND MONTGOMERY DO WHAT NO PAIR OF WHITE STOCKINGS EVER DID

The South Side's evening produced a first the franchise has waited a century and a quarter to record: Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery, who began the night tied at nine-and-twenty homers apiece, each struck his thirtieth against Minnesota — the first White Sox teammates ever to reach thirty in the same season in the same game, by the certification of the STATS bureau. Vargas claimed the bragging rights in the first inning; Montgomery answered with a two-run blow in the fourth; and between them Braden Montgomery — no relation, merely a namesake — added a homer of his own, the first time the two Montgomerys have gone deep in the same game. The clubhouse race remains crowded besides: Munetaka Murakami, whose American crossing these pages have chronicled, sits at nine-and-twenty and now trails both men by one. "Doing it on the same night and being able to share with Vargas is awesome," said the younger Montgomery, and the desk notes what the milestone serves: a young club, three seasons removed from hundred-loss misery, holding first place in September. The fuller account of the evening stands in the card below.

The Rest of the Card

THE NIGHTCAP OBLIGES IN KIND — BAZZANA LEVELS IT IN THE EIGHTH AND ENDS IT IN THE TENTH: GUARDIANS 4, BENGALS 3, IN TEN INNINGS

The day's second chapter matched the first beat for beat. Detroit built a 3-0 account on Kevin McGonigle's double and singles from Lee and Valencia; Cleveland answered by degrees — Nathaniel Lowe's double in the sixth, and in the eighth Travis Bazzana, who had entered only as a substitute when DeLauter's wrist sent him to the ward's columns, taking a 2-0 fastball 389 feet to center to level it at three. In the tenth, Rocchio — who else, on this of all days — stole second and then third, and Bazzana knocked a 2-2 cutter from Kenley Jansen up the middle to end it. The sweep is the club's first of a doubleheader by two walk-offs since the nineteenth of August, 1984, and no man needed it more than the rookie second baseman, whose August ran to a .566 OPS: "It's that time of year where you've got to make stuff happen," Bazzana said, "and this team does that." Gaddis took the decision; the Bengals, twice pierced in one day, have dropped seven of their last ten.

TEXAS STRIKES ITS FIRST GRAND SLAM OF THE YEAR AND LOSES ANYWAY, AS A TEN-GAME ROAD HOODOO DIES AT ARLINGTON: RAYS 7, RANGERS 6

Tampa Bay had lost ten consecutive road engagements with the Rangers — a hoodoo of genuine vintage — and buried it under a four-run fifth: Jonathan Aranda's ground-rule double, Junior Caminero's double behind it, Mesa's single, and a run cashed on a double play, all stacked upon earlier homers from Aranda and Richie Palacios. Whereupon Arlington nearly reclaimed the evening wholesale: Elias Díaz, batting with the bases full in the seventh, struck the Rangers' first grand slam of the entire season and added a ninth-inning sacrifice fly for five runs driven in. It wanted Caminero's run-scoring single in the top of that ninth to make the verdict stand, Wells sealing his sixth save behind Nick Martinez's fourteenth victory. The freight runs two ways: the Gulf Coast club banks its four-and-eightieth win on the day its ace entered the ward, as the columns above relate, while Texas — beaten with its biggest blow of the year — slips two games behind Cleveland's chair with the same clubs meeting again at 7:05 this evening, Rasmussen opposing deGrom.

FOUR RUNS BEFORE AN OUT OF CONSEQUENCE, AND THE CANADIANS CLIMB BACK TO LEVEL AT LAST: CANADIANS 9, ROYALS 2

Toronto spent the first inning of a ninety-seven-degree Kansas City evening settling the matter — Kirk and Okamoto singling home runs, Ernie Clement doubling home two more — and spent the rest of it padding the ledger: Kirk's double in the second, a sacrifice bunt cashed in the sixth ahead of George Springer's two-run double, and the rookie Sean Keys's second homer in the ninth, with Kirk, Clement, and Springer driving in two apiece. Bobby Witt Jr. and Vinnie Pasquantino supplied Kansas City's homers in a losing cause. The night's alarm was the starter Taillon's two-inning exit, the ward above having the particulars, and the reliever Mantiply took the decision in his stead. The sum is the story: at one-and-seventy wins against the same in defeats, the Canadians stand restored to level, winners of three running and seven of ten — and their reward is a place in the morning's tightest arithmetic, one game behind Cleveland's chair.

THREE RUNNERS CUT DOWN, ONE BALL LAUNCHED, AND THE LAST CHAIR CHANGES HANDS BY TEN O'CLOCK: MISSION NINE 3, PINSTRIPES 2, IN TEN INNINGS

The catcher Luis Campusano gave Petco Park a night for the annals: he threw out Grisham in the second, Chisholm in the fifth, and — after Spencer Jones's tenth-inning single had put New York ahead — cut down Jones himself at third with a perfect throw, before turning on the first pitch of the home half's decisive moment and launching a two-run walk-off homer off Blackburn. The scorers certify that only one other catcher since the leagues began keeping the count in 1951 has paired three runners caught stealing with a walk-off blast in one game: Sammy Taylor, in 1961. "You can't ask for more, honestly," ruled the manager Stammen. The visitors' evening deserves its own line: the piggyback of Max Fried and Will Warren, twice advertised in these pages, ran precisely to specification — Fried five and two-thirds bearing a single run, Warren two and a third without a hit — and was beaten anyway, Ben Rice's six-and-thirtieth homer the only other Pinstripe coin against Walker Buehler and the San Diego relief. The consequence sits atop the National's wild-card table: the Mission nine reclaim the last chair by half a game over Arizona, whose own quiet evening in Houston the card below relates.

HERRERA'S NINTH-INNING THUNDER TURNS SIX-FOUR INTO SEVEN-SIX, AND THE REDBIRDS ARE LEVEL ONCE MORE: CARDINALS 7, ROCKIES 6

Colorado had assembled its lead by the eccentric route the mountain air encourages — Cole Carrigg's two-run inside-the-park homer the jewel of a four-run sixth, Veen's squeeze bunt cashing another, and TJ Rumfield homering in the seventh, the third time in four mornings these pages have caught that man deciding or nearly deciding a game. St. Louis had answered with small coinage of its own, including the rookie Leo Bernal's first two-base hit and Jordan Walker's sacrifice that carried him to precisely one hundred runs driven in, third in the National behind clubmate Burleson's hundred and two. So it stood 6-4 against them in the ninth when Iván Herrera, facing the reliever Romano with two aboard, struck his fifteenth homer to center — three runs, the lead, and the game, O'Brien closing for his six-and-thirtieth save one night after these pages watched him blow one at Chavez Ravine. The Cardinals stand restored to level at one-and-seventy apiece, three and a half from the last chair; the Rockies, twice game and twice beaten this week, are owed better luck than September gives out.

THE APPOINTED DUEL KEEPS ITS APPOINTMENT THIS TIME — SALE OUTLASTS SÁNCHEZ AT THE SUMMIT OF THE EARNED-RUN TABLE: BRAVES 5, PHILLIES 2

Twice this week the desk has advertised a pitching card and once been made a fool for it; Friday in Philadelphia the pastime honored the bill. Chris Sale, second on the National's earned-run table at 2.10, gave six innings of two runs and seven strikeouts; Cristopher Sánchez, third at 2.58 and the league's leader in victories, matched him at six innings and was undone by his defense — a Harper error opening the gates on a three-run Atlanta second, Riley and Acuña singling home the honest portion. Alec Bohm supplied both Philadelphia runs with a double and a homer, and Mauricio Dubón closed the accounts with a two-run blast in the eighth, Iglesias sealing his thirtieth save. The standings turn the screw: Atlanta, winners of eight in ten, stretch the East's lead to five full games over the Phillies with the same clubs meeting at 6:05 this evening, Pérez opposing Wheeler — and the wild-card ledger now reads Chicago's top chair by a half-game over Philadelphia, a race within the race worth a morning eye.

NINE STRIKEOUTS, ONE DOUBLE, AND THE RESTORED PHENOM CROSSES WITH THE ONLY RUN OF THE NIGHT: SMOKY CITY NINE 1, SERAPHS 0

Pittsburgh's evening was economy itself: Jared Jones struck out nine across six innings of three hits, Dotel and Montgomery finished the whitewashing, and the game's entire scoring was transacted in the second, when Konnor Griffin — the twenty-year-old whose return from two months' exile these pages heralded yesterday — reached, ran, and came home on Jake Mangum's double. The restored man thus pays his first dividend within a day of the ward's discharge. The Seraphs, who mustered four hits and struck out twelve times, have now dropped three running and nine of ten — the sale of the franchise, this paper suspects, cannot close quickly enough for the Anaheim faithful — while the Smoky City nine bank a second consecutive victory and hold their September form at seven wins in ten games, with Ashcraft and his fourteen victories taking the hill against the same visitors at 6:40 this evening.

A FIRST-INNING BLAST, EIGHT INNINGS OF SILENCE, AND A FULL-DRESS FRACAS BESIDES: HUB NINE 1, ORIOLES 0

Mickey Gasper opened the evening at Camden Yards with a homer, his eighth, and the pitching declined to add another run all night: Ranger Suárez carried seven scoreless innings of five hits, Whitlock bridged the eighth, and Chapman shut the ninth for his two-and-thirtieth save while Baltimore's Baz bore a hard-luck loss. The theatre came between: after an inning-ending double play in the eighth, Blaze Alexander's slide into second drew stares, the stares drew words, and both benches and bullpens emptied onto the infield grass — warnings issued, nobody ejected, and the antagonists afterward the mildest men in Maryland. "Not a big deal, not a huge thing," ruled Boston's interim manager Tracy; "just two teams competing," agreed Baltimore's Albernaz. The standings are less forgiving than the testimony: the Orioles have lost four running, stand nought-and-four in September with their fifth whitewashing of the year, and have slipped three games from Cleveland's chair — while the Hub nine, twice winners running, keep the wild card's second chair in comfort. The clubs go again at 7:05 this evening, and the desk notes the visitors send Sonny Gray and his sixteen victories, the American's most, against Bassitt.

IMANAGA CARRIES SIX SPARE INNINGS UNDER THE CLOSED ROOF, AND THE FLORIDIANS FADE A LITTLE FURTHER: CUBS 6, FLORIDIANS 1

The Cubs' evening in Miami was a study in sufficiency: Shota Imanaga permitted three hits and a single run across six innings, Civale closed with three frames for a rare long save, and the scoring gathered without a single mighty blow until the ninth — a second-inning force out, then a sixth built of Ian Happ's bases-loaded walk, Nico Hoerner's single, and a sacrifice fly, with Pete Crow-Armstrong trotting home on a wild pitch in the seventh. Michael Busch's eighteenth homer dressed the final line. The center fielder the milestone desk sang all week added his eight-and-twentieth double and three-and-thirtieth stolen base, the forty-homer question still standing at one swing; the Floridians, held to four hits, drop a second straight and slip three and a half games from the National's last chair — the arithmetic that whispered to them a week ago now barely audible.

FIVE BALLS OVER THE FLUSHING FENCES, TWO OF THEM ALVAREZ'S: METS 10, FRISCO NINE 6

New York settled the argument in its first two turns at bat — Mark Vientos's three-run homer in the first, then a four-run second crowned by Francisco Alvarez's first blast and Bo Bichette's two-run drive, seven runs before San Francisco had its bearings — and kept the hammer handy thereafter, Francisco Lindor adding a two-run homer in the sixth and Alvarez his second of the night in the eighth: five over the fences in all. Nolan McLean rode the cushion to his eleventh victory with seven strikeouts. The visitors' account was very nearly all Rafael Devers: two doubles, a three-run homer — his three-and-thirtieth — and five runs driven in, magnificent and unavailing, the Frisco nine dropping a second straight in a season that has long since stopped keeping score of its indignities. The same clubs meet at 4:10 this afternoon, Molina opposing Thornton.

THE MILESTONE DESK'S BUSINESS IS TRANSACTED BY THE FOURTH INNING: PALE HOSE 4, MINNESOTANS 1

The evening's history stands in the news columns above — Vargas in the first, Braden Montgomery in the second, Colson Montgomery's two-run blow in the fourth, three homers doing all the scoring a first-place club required — and the pitching kept the ledger clean: Erick Fedde threw five scoreless innings on the season's most humid night, running his career account against Minnesota to five victories without a defeat and a 1.18 figure. "Maybe they just bring the best out of me," the pitcher allowed. Josh Bell's eighteenth homer in the ninth spoiled the shutout and nothing else. The Pale Hose thus open a six-game homestand by protecting what Cleveland's twin heroics had made precious: the Central's lead holds at two and a half games with one-and-twenty to play, and the Minnesotans, twice beaten running, recede toward the season's margins. The clubs resume at 7:10 this evening, Bradley opposing Kay.

JAVIER PERMITS ONE HIT IN FIVE, AND ARIZONA'S CHAIR IS GONE BY MIDNIGHT: HOUSTON NINE 3, DIAMONDBACKS 1

The evening under the Houston roof was settled in a single frame: Yainer Diaz's eleventh homer opened a three-run third, Isaac Paredes doubled home the second run, and Altuve's sacrifice fly cashed the third. Cristian Javier made it stand — one hit across five innings with eight strikeouts, the one hit being Gabriel Moreno's answering homer in the fourth — and four relievers carried the arrangement home, Josh Hader sealing his three-and-twentieth save. Arizona finished with three hits entire, and the toll was exacted elsewhere before it was counted at home: with San Diego's ten-o'clock heroics, the Diamondbacks surrender the National's last chair by half a game, the very seat this paper has watched change hands four times in a week. Houston, for its part, has won three running and holds the West by three full games over beaten Texas — a lead that stood at a single game on Wednesday's masthead.

FOUR BALLS LEAVE ONE INNING — MUNCY, WILLIAMS, McNEIL, AND GELOF IN PROCESSION — AND THE SPOILERS SPOIL AGAIN: ATHLETICS 7, MARINERS 6

The third inning at Seattle produced a curiosity the wires certify: four Athletic homers in the single frame — solo blasts from Max Muncy and Alika Williams, Jeff McNeil's two-run drive, and Zack Gelof's seventeenth in procession — five runs erasing an early deficit against Logan Gilbert, who struck out ten and was beaten anyway. Cal Raleigh's two-run homer dragged the home nine level at five, whereupon Gelof tripled and scored the tiebreaking runs' first in a two-run fifth, Butler singling him home. Naylor's eighth-inning knock closed the gap to one and no further, Harris sealing his fifteenth save. The Athletics have now won three running in the role September assigns a last-place club with self-respect — spoiler in the yards of the fading — while the Mariners, losers of seven in ten, watch a once-plausible September recede; the clubs meet again at 9:40 this evening.

SNELL THROWS SIX SPOTLESS AND TUCKER REMEMBERS THE FENCES: TROLLEY DODGERS 5, WASHINGTONS 3

The champions' evening ran to the old specifications: Blake Snell carried six scoreless innings of five hits and seven strikeouts, the third inning banked three on Mookie Betts's run-scoring single and Teoscar Hernández's two-run double — that man's bat still warm from Thursday's heroics in these pages — and in the sixth Kyle Tucker struck his twelfth homer, his first baseball over a fence since the eighth of August, a drought of nearly a month ended to the visible relief of Chavez Ravine. Washington's answer came all in the ninth — three runs on James Wood's double and singles around it — close enough to require Dreyer's second save, no closer. The great Ohtani rested a second consecutive night, as the ward relates, and the champions scarcely missed him: at four-and-eighty wins they hold the West by ten full games, and receive the Washingtons again at 9:10 this evening with Glasnow and his 2.79 taking the hill against Cavalli.

DOWN TWO IN THE FIFTH, THE LEAGUE'S BEST ANSWER WITH FIVE — PRATT'S TRIPLE CLEARS THE BASES: MILWAUKEES 10, REDLEGS 7

Cincinnati built its lead with proper thunder — Matt McLain's two-run homer in the second, Eugenio Suárez's three-run blast in the third, six runs on the board against four — and Milwaukee dismantled it with the patient tools that have built the game's best ledger, eight-and-eighty wins now against four-and-fifty defeats. The fifth told the tale: Turang struck by a pitch with the bases full, then Cooper Pratt — twenty years old, playing shortstop for the best team in baseball — clearing them with a triple to right and trotting home himself on a wild pitch, five runs in the frame and a season-high four driven in for the young man. William Contreras doubled home the tenth in the sixth, Brice Turang finished with three runs batted in, and Megill struck out the side in the ninth for his six-and-twentieth save. The Redlegs' consolations were real — Sal Stewart's run-scoring single carried the majors' leading count to one hundred six, the freshman total these pages have sung since August — but the arithmetic holds: Milwaukee leads the Central by eight, and the clubs go again at 6:40 this evening, May opposing Abbott.

First the standings, then tonight's bill. In the American: Tampa Bay's lead in the East is four over New York, with Boston seven and a half astern; the White Sox keep the Central by two and a half over doubly-triumphant Cleveland; Houston holds the West by three over Texas. The wild-card row reads New York and Boston comfortable, and then the morning's crush: Cleveland's last chair at two-and-seventy wins, Toronto — level at last — one game behind, Texas two, and reeling Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta by five over Philadelphia; Milwaukee, still the game's best ledger, by eight over Chicago; Los Angeles by ten over San Diego — and the last chair returned overnight to the Mission nine by half a game over Arizona, with Miami and St. Louis three and a half back and the top of that row its own race besides, Chicago holding first chair by a half-game over the Phillies. Tonight's card runs to fifteen engagements, all verified against the schedule, and the desk directs the eye to five: at 6:05 in Philadelphia the East's leaders press their advantage, Pérez opposing Wheeler; at 6:10 in Cleveland the walk-off heroes receive Detroit once more, Messick and his 2.46 against Valdez; at 7:05 in Baltimore the American's winningest arm takes the hill, Gray and his sixteen victories opposing Bassitt; at 7:05 in Arlington the Rays and Rangers resume their argument, Rasmussen against deGrom; and at 7:15 in San Diego the Pinstripes seek their remedy for the catcher's midnight thunder, Rodón opposing Ray. The night owls are commended to Seattle at 9:40, where the spoilers of the third inning try for four straight. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~
