entry.title: A MINUTE'S OVATION FROM THE CITY THAT TRADED HIM, THEN TWO HOMERS AGAINST ITS COLORS: RUTSCHMAN RETURNS TO CAMDEN YARDS: RED SOX 6, ORIOLES 5
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 58 · Friday, the Fourth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 9 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

A MINUTE'S OVATION FROM THE CITY THAT TRADED HIM, THEN TWO HOMERS AGAINST ITS COLORS: RUTSCHMAN RETURNS TO CAMDEN YARDS: RED SOX 6, ORIOLES 5

One month to the day after the deadline deal that sent the ultimate Oriole north, Adley Rutschman stands in at his old harbor to a standing ovation of nearly a minute — then strikes towering solo blasts in the first and the sixth, Roman Anthony's ninth-inning drive supplies the winning run, and Chapman survives a two-run answer to close a seven-homer evening

Baltimore spent the better part of a minute Thursday evening telling Adley Rutschman what he had meant to it, and Rutschman spent the rest of the night showing the city what it had let go. The first man taken in the whole of the 2019 draft, an Oriole and nothing else his entire professional life until the third of August — when a deal struck hours before the deadline sent him to Boston, of all places, a rival within the division — he returned to Camden Yards for the first time wearing the visitors' flannels. The club played a tribute upon the videoboard; the grandstand rose and stayed risen for close to a minute as he dug in; and the man himself called it what it was: "Just to feel that love was a really cool, emotional moment, and really special." Then he compartmentalized, in his own word, and before the first inning was done had put the baseball over the fence.

That first-inning blast was his tenth of the season, and the sixth-inning copy his eleventh — two towering solo shots from a catcher who had missed the three previous games entire with the hyperextended right elbow this paper's ward has been tracking, an ailment the club concedes will want managing to the season's end. "That's a heck of a way to make a return," said Boston's interim manager Chad Tracy, who had watched the ovation from the dugout and pronounced the home club's gesture first-class. Between Rutschman's bookends the contest swung properly: Pete Alonso answered the first blow with a sacrifice fly, and in the fourth Luis Robert Jr. and Alonso struck homers in the same frame — the latter's three-and-thirtieth, the man standing joint first in the American in runs driven home at four-and-ninety — to put Baltimore ahead. Boston drew level on Isiah Kiner-Falefa's seventh-inning single, went ahead on Nick Sogard's two-run drive in the eighth, and banked the run that proved the difference when the rookie Roman Anthony opened the ninth with his third homer. It was wanted: Christian Encarnacion-Strand struck a two-run blow off Chapman in the home ninth before the closer shut the door on his one-and-thirtieth save — seven baseballs over the fences in all, nine of the evening's eleven runs riding upon them. The win fell to the reliever Miller, the loss to De León.

The standings read the evening two ways. Boston, at six-and-seventy wins, sits securely in the wild-card row's second chair; Baltimore has now dropped three running, and stands a game and a half from the last chair with the scrum above it tightening by the day, as the card below relates. But the arithmetic was not really the story, and everyone in the yard knew it. The story went home wearing road grey, having answered a month of upheaval with the finest kind of correspondence: two letters, both delivered over the wall.

News Around the League

THE LAUREL DESK: AUGUST'S GARLANDS ARE DISTRIBUTED — CAGLIANONE AND CROW-ARMSTRONG TAKE THE PLAYERS' PALMS, AND BOTH ANSWER THE HONOR THE SAME EVENING

The league published its August honors Thursday, and the two headline laurels went to young men who promptly justified them by nightfall. The American's Player of the Month is Kansas City's Jac Caglianone, three-and-twenty years old, whose .411 August average and 1.113 OPS led all baseball — the first Royal so honored since Bobby Witt Jr. in the July of 2024 — and who marked the announcement with two hits and two runs driven in against Miami, as the card below relates. The National's palm goes to the Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong, his second of the season, earned with a fourteen-homer August that led the majors and helped Chicago to a record no National League club had ever posted: two-and-sixty home runs in a single calendar month. He celebrated by striking his nine-and-thirtieth of the year to beat Milwaukee, the milestone desk below having more to say on that number.

The pitching palms went to Kansas City's Noah Cameron in the American — a 1.87 August ERA with a one-hit shutout of the Angels in it — and Philadelphia's Jesús Luzardo in the National, whose 1.31 figure and six-and-forty strikeouts in four-and-thirty innings and a third continued the summer this paper has watched him assemble. The freshman honors: the White Sox outfielder Tristan Peters, once of the barnstorming Savannah Bananas and now a first-place club's everyday revelation, took the American's rookie palm with a 1.054 OPS; Cincinnati's Sal Stewart, who leads all baseball at one hundred five runs driven in, took the National's. And the relief awards went to a pair of perfect ledgers: Houston's Josh Hader, unscored upon for the whole of August and a spotless one-and-twenty for one-and-twenty in save chances this season, and Milwaukee's Trevor Megill, eight for eight in August with opponents batting .053 against him. The Herald extends its congratulations, and notes with approval that the hardware desk and the box scores are, for once, in perfect agreement.

THE RUMORS DESK: THE METROPOLITANS' EYES TURN ACROSS THE PACIFIC — STEARNS SEEN IN THE STANDS IN JAPAN AS THE SLUGGER SATO WEIGHS THE CROSSING

The winter's first great courtship acquires a sighting. Teruaki Sato, the left-handed slugger of Japan's Hanshin Tigers — the Central League's Most Valuable Player of 2025, forty homers and a hundred and two driven in that season, and two-and-thirty more homers this year with an OPS above a thousand — may come to these shores through the posting system this offseason, and the wire desks report the Mets, Yankees, Dodgers, and Phillies among the clubs linked to him, per the chronicler Heyman of the New York Post. The freshest evidence is the most concrete: the Mets' president of baseball operations David Stearns was seen in attendance Wednesday at the Hanshin nine's engagement with the Yakult Swallows, where Sato obliged the scout in the stands by striking his two-and-thirtieth homer of the year.

The particulars, all duly hedged as reports: Sato is seven-and-twenty, has manned third base for the bulk of his Japanese career, and might be asked to cross the diamond to first were he to land in Queens — the path already walked by the White Sox's Munetaka Murakami, another Japanese third baseman now stationed at first on the South Side and sitting on nine-and-twenty homers in his first American summer. The desk files the story where it files all September courtship: promising, unconsummated, and worth watching when the posting window opens. The reader will note which clubs' names appear in it — the game's great purses, assembled around one bat — and draw the customary conclusions about where the winter's bidding shall be loudest.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE GREAT OHTANI TAKES A NIGHT IN THE PARLOR, CHICAGO'S BROWN IS DONE FOR THE YEAR, AND PITTSBURGH EXPECTS ITS PHENOM BACK THIS VERY EVENING

The ward's ledger opens again in Los Angeles, where Shohei Ohtani was held from the batting order Thursday, one night after four strikeouts and a visible wince told the story his manager then confirmed. Roberts owns that the man is "not 100%" upon the mound either — the catalogue runs to the left knee, the right biceps, and what the skipper calls the overall body — though the club yet hopes he pitches again this season, and his return to the lineup is a day-to-day question. His stand-in atop the order, the ward notes with approval, filled the post to the tune of four hits, as the card below sings.

In Chicago the news is harder: the Cubs' right-hander Ben Brown will not pitch again this year. The trouble is a stress reaction in a bone of the neck — the fifth vertebra, by the pitcher's own account — the same affliction that claimed the last three months of his 2024, and a rehabilitation outing of late August brought the discomfort back. "After consulting with doctors, it's just more rest," said the manager Counsell, with the weariness of a man prescribing patience to an athlete. The focus shifts to 2027, and the ward wishes the young man a winter of genuine healing.

Pittsburgh, by contrast, prepares to make a withdrawal from the ward rather than a deposit: the twenty-year-old phenom Konnor Griffin, absent since the fifth of July, is expected to be activated for this evening's opener against the Angels — "He's a huge piece of the offense, defense, baserunning, everything," says the manager Kelly, committing to nothing while telegraphing everything. The surging Buccaneers' account of themselves stands in the card below; the ward merely observes that reinforcements rarely arrive at a better-chosen hour.

THE MILESTONE DESK: CROW-ARMSTRONG STANDS ONE BLOW SHY OF FORTY, A SINGLE HOMER BEHIND SCHWARBER'S CROWN

The number nine-and-thirty deserves a column of its own. Pete Crow-Armstrong's Thursday homer — struck, the trackers certify, off a changeup barely more than a foot above the earth, the lowest pitch he has cleared a fence with all year — brings the Cubs' center fielder within one blow of the forty-homer threshold, a figure no man reaches by accident and few reach at all while also stealing two-and-thirty bases, as he has. Ahead of him on the National's table stands only Philadelphia's Kyle Schwarber at forty even; behind him, Atlanta's Olson at seven-and-thirty and Colorado's Goodman at six-and-thirty. The desk notes besides that Crow-Armstrong ranks among the National's leaders in runs driven in at three-and-ninety and in stolen bases alike, which is why the letters M-V-P attach themselves to his name in every wire dispatch the Herald skims. Three-and-twenty days remain to the season; the arithmetic wants one swing for forty, and the race for the National's home-run crown wants watching every morning between now and the seven-and-twentieth.

THE ALMANAC DESK: CLEMENTE'S DAY IS APPOINTED FOR THE FIFTEENTH, AND THE SEASON'S LAST PAGE FOR THE SEVEN-AND-TWENTIETH

The desk sets down the calendar's fixed stars, each verified against the schedule-keepers at Baseball-Reference. Roberto Clemente Day falls on the fifteenth of September, when all thirty clubs honor the great Pittsburgh right fielder and humanitarian — a date this paper marks each year with particular feeling, the man having been the deadball virtues incarnate a generation after the deadball age. The regular season's final page is the seven-and-twentieth of September, three-and-twenty days from this morning's masthead; the wild-card series open two days later, on the nine-and-twentieth; the division series follow on the third of October, the league championships on the eleventh and twelfth, and the World Series on the three-and-twentieth, with provision made for a seventh game as late as the very eve of November. Between this morning and that last page stand the scrums the desk note below enumerates — three clubs within a game and a half of the American's last chair, three within four games of the National's — and the Herald commends the almanac to any reader tempted to look away for even a weekend.

The Rest of the Card

FIVE RUNS AND NOT ONE OF THEM DRIVEN HOME BY A HIT: BUCCANEERS 5, JINTS 2

Pittsburgh took the set from San Francisco by a method the scorers will be explaining for a week: five runs, and not a single one of them cashed by a base hit. The ledger reads a bases-loaded walk to Oneil Cruz, a bases-loaded plunking of Jake Mangum, a sacrifice bunt turned run by a throwing error, a force-out challenge overturned in Pittsburgh's favor, and Jared Triolo's sacrifice fly — an inventory of small coinage that a bullpen day made stand up, the decision falling to Khristian Curtis, recalled from Indianapolis only that morning, with Montgomery sealing his eighth save. The visitors' whole account was a two-run seventh built on Jung Hoo Lee's double. It is the Buccaneers' fifth series win in their last six tries — "the fight in this team is real," testifies Mangum, and the wild-card arithmetic, though still unkind, has stopped laughing — and the ward above has the gladder news besides: the phenom Griffin is expected back in the lineup this very evening against the Angels.

FOUR IN THE FIFTH SETTLE THE AFTERNOON, AND TORONTO POCKETS THE TIEBREAKER BESIDES: TORONTOS 6, FOREST CITY NINE 3

The set's finale in Cleveland went to the visitors on one crowded fifth inning: Nathan Lukes's two-run double the heavy freight, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. adding a sacrifice fly and Jesús Sánchez a run-scoring single — four runs where the home nine had led. Cleveland's answer, two in the home half on Austin Hedges's single, was the last of it; Ernie Clement singled home the sixth run in the ninth, Miles took the decision, and the loss fell to Bibee. The freight the game carried outweighed the game: the win closes Toronto's account with Cleveland at four games to two this season, and by the tiebreaking rules that head-to-head verdict could prove the season's most valuable coin — the Torontos stand this morning a half-game from the very chair the Forest City nine still hold, with Texas level beside them and Baltimore a game astern. "I loved the way we bounced back," said the manager Schneider, whose club has won six of ten and proceeds to Kansas City tonight.

ALTUVE STRIKES FIRST AND VARSHO TRIPLES THE ARGUMENT HOME: ASTROS 6, WHITE SOX 2

The evening under Houston's roof belonged to the home nine from the second pitch of consequence: Jose Altuve's two-run homer, his fifteenth, before an out had been recorded. Chicago drew level in the second on singles from Rogers and Antonacci, whereupon the third settled everything — Isaac Paredes's run-scoring double, Daulton Varsho's two-run triple, and Christian Walker's single, four runs in the frame. Hunter Brown did the rest: six innings, two runs, seven strikeouts for his fifth victory, the bullpen finishing without incident while Castillo bore the loss. The Space City club has won seven of ten and holds the West by two games over Texas, with the wire desks now openly discussing the American's second seed; the White Sox, twice beaten running, nonetheless keep the Central by three over Cleveland — whose afternoon the card above chronicles — and the season series between these leaders concluded with honors worth counting come tiebreak time.

GAUSMAN AND HENDERSON DUEL AT SEVEN INNINGS APIECE, AND CROW-ARMSTRONG'S THIRTY-NINTH DECIDES IT: BRUINS 2, SUDS MEN 1

The Wrigley argument's fourth and final chapter produced the pitching the first three withheld. Logan Henderson gave Milwaukee seven innings of three hits and seven strikeouts and was beaten; Kevin Gausman — the deadline acquisition doing precisely the office he was acquired for — gave Chicago seven innings of five hits and nine strikeouts and was not. The difference was two runs in the third: Pete Crow-Armstrong reached down for a changeup scarcely a foot off the ground and sent it to dead center at better than a hundred and four miles to the hour, his nine-and-thirtieth of the season, with Carson Kelly aboard. Andrew Vaughn's answering solo blast in the fourth was Milwaukee's entire account, and Rolison closed the ninth for his second save. "Absolutely dominant," ruled Crow-Armstrong of his pitcher, and the arithmetic ruled the set a draw: two games apiece, the Central's gap holding at eight, and the Suds men — beaten with but five hits by a club that managed only three — reminded that the best record in baseball buys no immunity at Wrigley Field. The milestone desk above weighs what the young center fielder's number means; his club merely banks the win and sails for Miami.

JENSEN'S MOONSHOT SAILS FOUR HUNDRED AND FORTY FEET INTO THE ROYAL ANNALS: KANSAS CITY NINE 7, GULF STREAM NINE 3

The friendly rivalry this paper glimpsed Wednesday — the rookie catcher chasing his clubmate's homer count — added its next chapter at Kauffman Stadium. Carter Jensen, who homered twice in Wednesday's losing cause as these pages recorded, tripled in the third and in the fifth struck a go-ahead two-run blast the trackers measured at four hundred forty feet: his two-and-twentieth of the year, his third in two nights, and a figure matching Bo Jackson's 1987 and Carlos Beltrán's 1999 for the second-most ever by a Royals rookie, two shy of Bob Hamelin's four-and-twenty. Jac Caglianone, crowned the American's Player of the Month that very day as the laurel desk relates, answered with a game-tying double and a run-scoring single — "I've got to freaking start hitting homers," the man protested, guarding his one-homer lead in the clubhouse race — and a three-run eighth built on Salvador Perez's and Vinnie Pasquantino's doubles closed the accounts. Wacha took the decision over Alcantara. Miami's portion was a leadoff homer from Heriberto Hernández, his three-and-twentieth, and Agustín Ramírez's solo blow; the Gulf Stream nine thus slip three games from the National's last chair with the season running short, while last-place Kansas City, at three-and-sixty wins, plays September for 2027 — and on Thursday's evidence, 2027 answers.

QUANTRILL THROWS SEVEN CLEAN, AND THE AMERICAN'S BEST ARE BLANKED ON THREE HITS: TEXAS NINE 6, SUNSHINE NINE 0

Arlington handed the league's best record a whitewashing. Cal Quantrill carried a seldom-used slider through seven innings of two hits and five strikeouts — the wire desks report the pitch has quietly become his September weapon — and Tampa Bay finished the night with three hits entire, McClanahan bearing the loss. The scoring gathered by degrees: Foscue's single in the fourth, Duran's in the fifth ahead of Corey Seager's two-run homer, his fourteenth, and a two-run eighth on Evan Carter's triple and Jake Burger's sacrifice fly. The consequences run in two directions at once. The Sunshine nine have now dropped two straight, though their lead in the East holds at three games over the Yankees; the Texas nine, for their part, climb within a half-game of the American's last chair — level in the loss column with the Torontos, whose own afternoon the card above relates — and the same clubs go again at 8:05 this evening with the scrum growing less theoretical by the hour.

DOWN THREE BEFORE AN OUT WAS BANKED, AND EVERY RUN RECOVERED WITH INTEREST: WHITE ELEPHANTS 7, SEATTLE NINE 4

Seattle scored three times before recording an out of its own first inning — Julio Rodríguez's double, Cal Raleigh's single, and a knock from the celebrated debutant Montes, whose arrival the debut desk sang on Wednesday — and had been outplayed thoroughly by the ninth. The visitors' answer ran to fourteen hits: Zack Gelof's leadoff homer to open the game, his sixteenth, Lawrence Butler's two-run single in the fifth, Donovan Walton's go-ahead blast in the sixth, and insurance from Muncy and Jeff McNeil in the late innings, Blewett winning in relief and Harris sealing his fourteenth save. The sixth inning supplied the theatre: directly after Walton's homer, the reliever Vargas ran a cutter up and in to strike Brian Serven, the umpire Hoye gathered his crew and warned both benches, and Seattle's manager Dan Wilson, emerging to ask why, was ejected for the asking — his fourth removal of the season, the most by a Mariners manager since 2022. "I was looking for an explanation," said Wilson afterward, still without one. The Elephants have won two running in the yard of a fading club; the Seattle nine have lost six of their last ten and their manager's patience besides.

THE NATIONAL'S SAVES LEADER IS TOUCHED FOR TWO WITH THE GAME IN HIS HANDS, AND TEOSCAR SENDS THE RAVINE HOME HAPPY: DODGERS 3, MOUND CITY NINE 2

The finale at Chavez Ravine turned on one full-count sinker. St. Louis had led since the first — run-scoring singles from the young Joshua Báez and Ramón Urías building a 2-0 account, twelve hits in all against a Dodger six — and Skubal, touched for ten hits without one of them going for extra bases, had kept the champions within reach at two runs through the middle innings; a fifth-inning wild pitch brought Edman home for their first coin. So it stood at 2-1 into the ninth, when Riley O'Brien — the National's saves leader at five-and-thirty, whose five-and-thirtieth closed Wednesday's account in these very pages — was asked for one more. Edman singled, Betts walked, and Teoscar Hernández crushed the 3-2 sinker to the gap in left-center: both runners home, the game over, the blown save O'Brien's sixth. It was the champions' only hit of the night with a runner in scoring position — they had gone hitless in their previous four-and-twenty such chances across two evenings — and Tommy Edman, keeping the leadoff post while the great Ohtani rested as the ward relates, supplied four of the six hits himself. "Teo came through huge," said Edman, and the tables agree: the Dodgers salvage the set's last game at three-and-eighty wins, while the Mound City nine, restored to level only Wednesday, slip a game under it once more — the season's cruelest denomination of coin, spent twice in two days.

The tables on the fourth morning of September, taken in one turning. In the American: Tampa Bay's lead in the East is three over New York, with Boston seven and a half astern; the White Sox keep the Central by three over Cleveland; Houston holds the West by two over Texas. The wild-card row reads New York and Boston comfortable — and then the morning's best theatre, tighter by a half-game than yesterday: Cleveland's last chair at seventy wins and seventy defeats, with Texas and Toronto a half-game behind, Baltimore a game and a half, and Minnesota three. In the National: Atlanta by four over Philadelphia; Milwaukee, still owner of the game's best ledger, by eight over Chicago; Los Angeles by nine and a half over Arizona — and the last chair Arizona's by half a game over San Diego, with Miami three back and St. Louis four. Tonight's card runs to sixteen engagements — a twin bill in Cleveland among them, the Tigers visiting at 2:10 and again at 7:15 — all verified against the schedule, and the desk directs the eye to four: at 6:40 in Philadelphia the month's handsomest pitching card, Sale and his 2.06 opposing Sánchez and his sixteen victories, the second and third names on the National's earned-run table meeting head-on; at 6:45 in Pittsburgh the Angels arrive as the phenom Griffin is expected back in Buccaneer flannels; at 8:05 in Arlington the Sunshine nine seek their remedy for last night's whitewashing, Martinez opposing Williams; and at 9:40 in San Diego the Yankees at last unveil the Fried-and-Warren piggyback these pages have twice advertised, Buehler standing against it. The night owls are commended to Chavez Ravine at 10:10, where Snell takes the hill for the champions against the capital club. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: TWICE IN THE ELEVENTH THE BIRDS REACH SAFE HARBOR, AND TWICE THE MOUNTAIN MEN PULL THEM BACK OUT TO SEA: ROCKIES 6, BIRDS 5, IN ELEVEN INNINGS
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 57 · Thursday, the Third of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWICE IN THE ELEVENTH THE BIRDS REACH SAFE HARBOR, AND TWICE THE MOUNTAIN MEN PULL THEM BACK OUT TO SEA: ROCKIES 6, BIRDS 5, IN ELEVEN INNINGS

Baltimore builds a three-run third, watches Colorado erase it by instalments through nine, seizes the lead afresh with two in the eleventh — and surrenders three in the bottom half, Brett Sullivan's two-run single closing the accounts of a Coors Field marathon that somehow produced eleven runs without one ball leaving the yard

No club in either league owes September less than Colorado. The Mountain men woke Wednesday more than eight-and-twenty games out of the West's race, six-and-eighty times beaten, playing for nothing but the pleasure of the thing — while Baltimore, a game under .500 and a game and a half from the American's last wild-card chair, played for everything the month can still give. The pastime, which delights in such asymmetries, arranged for the club with nothing at stake to win its second straight from the club with everything at stake, and to do it twice over in a single eleventh inning.

The Birds had begun properly enough: a three-run third on Pete Alonso's run-scoring single — his two-and-ninetieth driven in, second in all the American — and Luis Robert Jr.'s two-run double. Colorado's reply came a run at a time, and once by decree: Jake McCarthy's third-inning triple scored Amador, but McCarthy himself, waved home behind the ball, was ruled safe until Baltimore's challenge overturned the call at the plate. Cole Carrigg singled home a run in the fourth, and in the ninth, with the account still 3-2 against them, Zac Veen doubled home Carrigg to force the extra chapters. In the eleventh Baltimore did what a contender must: run-scoring singles from Samuel Basallo and Blaze Alexander, a 5-3 lead, the harbor lights in view. Whereupon the home half undid it entire — TJ Rumfield, whose Tuesday drive won the previous evening's contest as this paper recorded, singled home the first run, and Sullivan lined a single to left with two aboard, both runners scoring, the ledger reading six to five and the set to Colorado.

The win fell to Castaño, the loss to Wolfram, and the arithmetic falls hardest on the visitors: the Birds stand two under at nine-and-sixty wins against one-and-seventy defeats, still a game and a half behind Cleveland's chair — for the Guardians, beaten eleven to nothing in their own yard as the card below relates, contrived to concede not an inch of ground — and now share the pursuers' row at that identical figure with Texas and Toronto, three clubs pressed shoulder to shoulder against one door. Colorado, for its part, has now won two running, and the eleven-run evening's curiosity bears repeating: in the yard where the baseball flies thinnest of air, not one cleared the fence.

News Around the League

THE MILESTONE DESK: ACUÑA STRIKES HIS TWO-HUNDREDTH HOMER AND STANDS ALONE IN THE ANNALS — NO MAN EVER PAIRED TWO HUNDRED WITH TWO HUNDRED STEALS SO FAST

In the seventh inning of Wednesday's rout in the capital, Ronald Acuña Jr. jumped upon a first-pitch fastball from the Nationals' reliever Max Kranick and deposited it 379 feet into the bullpen walkway in left — a three-run blow, his two-hundredth career homer, and with it a record all his own: in his 904th game, Acuña becomes the fastest man in the history of the majors to pair two hundred homers with two hundred stolen bases, five-and-twenty games quicker than Alfonso Soriano managed the double. The names next on that list read like a gallery wing — Eric Davis, Bobby Bonds, Sammy Sosa, Barry Bonds — and the new leader received the honor with becoming modesty: "For me, it's an honor to be on that list with Alfonso Soriano." His manager Weiss put it plainer: "It's freakish talent."

The milestone had kept the man waiting sixteen games since his last homer in mid-August, a stretch in which he batted a spare .207; he answered Wednesday with three hits in five turns and his two-hundred-twenty-fifth career steal already banked. The fuller demolition his club visited upon Washington stands in the card below, and the calendar now hands the champion-elect of the East a proper test: a four-game engagement at Philadelphia opening Friday evening. "I love to play against Philly," said Acuña. "This weekend, it's like playoff games."

THE OWNERSHIP DESK, CONTINUED: THE PRICE OF THE ANGELS SURFACES AT FOUR THOUSAND MILLIONS, AND THE PAPERWORK BEGINS ITS SLOW MARCH

The sale this paper recorded yesterday morning acquires its figures. The gentlemen of ESPN, consulting their sources, report that Stan Kroenke's agreement to purchase the Angels from Arte Moreno runs to some four billion dollars — a sum the Herald sets beside every owner's cry of hardship at the bargaining table, and files for future reference. The wire desks supply besides the machinery of the thing: the agreement goes first to the league's executive ownership committee for review of the financials, then to a vote of the owners requiring three-quarters' assent — three-and-twenty of the nine-and-twenty — with the closing expected in the first quarter of 2027. The Herald also commends to the reader one detail of the purchaser's pedigree: the man's full name is Enos Stanley Kroenke, his parents having named him for two Cardinals, Enos Slaughter and Stan Musial. Whether a christening constitutes a baseball philosophy, Anaheim will discover.

Within the club, the wires report business proceeding as usual — the team president Molly Jolly and the interim general manager John Mozeliak both professing surprise at the timing and no contact yet with the Kroenke concern. Mozeliak's own engagement expires in December, and the search for a permanent general manager now waits upon the new proprietor's wishes; the veteran executive allows only that he has not decided his future. The club marked the second day of its new era by losing in ten innings, as the card below relates.

THE LABOR QUESTION: THE LEAGUE SKETCHES A CLOCK FOR THE HOT STOVE, WHILE THE PLAYERS SPEAK NAMELESSLY OF THE CAP AND THE SEASON AFTER NEXT

Two dispatches on matters of the purse crossed the wire this week, and the Herald reads them together. The first, from the league's friendly chroniclers: a proposal circulating to compress the winter's free-agent trade into two appointed windows — the first opening with the Winter Meetings in early December and closing at five o'clock on the one-and-twentieth, the second resuming the first Monday of February — with a freeze on signings between. The argument runs that the Hot Stove moves at a glacier's pace and that concentration would restore the Winter Meetings to a carnival, as the pitch clock restored briskness to the game itself. The second dispatch: ESPN has printed a canvass of players, speaking without their names attached, upon the salary-cap question, the bargaining to come, and whether there will be a 2027 season at all.

The Herald's sympathies in these columns are long declared and rest where they always have, with the men who play the games. It notes only this: the calendar proposal issues from the league office, and any scheme that tells a workingman when he may sell his labor deserves reading twice — once for the showmanship, once for the fine print. That the players must canvass anonymously on the question of whether next year's season will be played at all tells the reader more about the weather ahead than any proposal's prospectus. The desk will report the facts of both as they harden; its lean, as ever, it does not disguise.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: BOSTON'S CATCHING CORPS THINS BY TWO, AND IN LOS ANGELES THE GREAT OHTANI IS VISIBLY MORTAL

The ward's ledger runs coast to coast this morning. In Boston, Adley Rutschman sat out a third consecutive day with the hyperextended right elbow that the club now concedes will require management for the remainder of the season, and his fellow catcher Willson Contreras rests on the ten-day invalid list with the left hamstring he strained in the last days of August — the Crimson Hose, four and a half games secure in the wild-card row but twice beaten running, proceeding with the position patched.

In Los Angeles the concern wears the game's most famous face. Shohei Ohtani went hitless Wednesday, struck out four times, and was seen to shake out his right arm and wince — prompting his manager Roberts to a candor managers rarely volunteer: "I think that tonight was kind of the tip of the iceberg. But I've seen it over the last couple weeks, where he hasn't been who he is." A day's rest, or several, is on the table when player, manager, and trainers confer; the invalid list, Roberts believes, is not. The same club dispatched the pitcher Eric Lauer to the list with inflammation of the left elbow, and so the champions limp toward October counting the days until whole. The ward extends its customary wish: swift knitting to every name above.

THE VESTIBULE DESK, CONCLUDED: SALAS DONS THE TOOLS AT LAST — THE YOUNGEST MAN TO CATCH A MAJOR-LEAGUE GAME SINCE PUDGE RODRÍGUEZ

The door this paper has held open all week finally swung. Ethan Salas, whose airport odyssey and dugout apprenticeship the vestibule desk chronicled these last two mornings, caught Wednesday's contest in Cincinnati start to finish — and at twenty years of age stands as the youngest man to catch a major-league game since Iván Rodríguez in 1991, precisely as this paper foretold he would be. The bat offered nothing on the day — hitless in four turns, twice struck out — but no debut catcher was ever measured by his first afternoon's hitting, and the assignment itself, a September game bearing on his club's wild-card life, says what San Diego thinks of the young man's glove. That the Friars lost the game, and with it the set, is the card's business below; the vestibule desk closes its file content, and hands Master Salas over to the regular columns.

The Rest of the Card

MURPHY AND ACUÑA SUPPLY THE THUNDER, THE BULLPEN A TWO-HIT SILENCE, AND THE CAPITAL NINE ARE BLANKED: BRAVES 9, CAPITAL NINE 0

Atlanta avenged its two earlier stumblings in Washington with a shutout of clinical completeness: two hits allowed all evening, the reliever Elieser Hernández — a man summoned from the minors only that morning — carrying three spotless frames for the victory. The scoring waited upon the sixth, when Sean Murphy struck a three-run homer, and gathered weight from there: Acuña's milestone three-run blow in the seventh, which the desk above sings at proper length, Austin Riley's two-run single in the eighth, and Murphy again cashing a fourth run home in the ninth — four driven in for the catcher on the night. At three-and-eighty wins the Braves lead the East by four over Philadelphia, whose Friday appointment with them now carries the week's heaviest freight.

FIVE BALLS LEAVE ARLINGTON BEARING ATHLETIC INSIGNIA, TWO OF THEM BOLTE'S: A'S 9, ARLINGTON MEN 2

The other cellar club of the American's West chose the same evening as Colorado to play spoiler. Texas banked early homers from Ezequiel Duran and Justin Foscue and then watched the visitors strike five: Henry Bolte twice — four driven in on the night — with Zack Gelof, Jonah Heim, and Alika Williams filing in behind — nine unanswered runs in an evening that also found room for an hour-and-twenty-six-minute rain delay. Lopez took the victory, Bradford the loss, and the damage to the home nine is counted in the standings: at nine-and-sixty wins against one-and-seventy defeats the Arlington men fall level with Toronto and Baltimore in the scrum a game and a half behind Cleveland — three pursuers, one chair, and four-and-twenty days to settle it.

PAINTER THROWS SEVEN SPOTLESS AND LOSES; McCANN'S ONE SWING TAKES THE LAST CHAIR: DESERT NINE 1, QUAKERS 0

The afternoon in the desert produced the day's leanest arithmetic: three hits for each side, one run between them, and that run struck in the eighth by James McCann, a fly ball to left off the reliever Bowlan. It wasted a performance of genuine cruelty to waste — the young Andrew Painter carrying seven scoreless innings of two hits and six strikeouts for Philadelphia, whose six-game winning streak dies at the door of a bullpen day: seven Arizona pitchers passed the baton through a three-hit shutout, Loáisiga taking the decision and Morillo the save. The consequences ran both directions. The Quakers surrender a game of their wild-card cushion, now five and a half; the Desert nine, at four-and-seventy wins, seize sole title to the National's last chair, half a game ahead of the Friars — the very chair this paper watched them slip from only yesterday.

TWO FOUR-RUN INNINGS UNDER THE CLOSED ROOF, AND THE SET GOES TO THE SOUND: PUGET SOUND MEN 8, CRIMSON HOSE 3

Seattle settled the rubber match in two instalments — four runs in the third on singles thick as herring, Josh Naylor's two-run knock the heaviest, and four more in the sixth, Dominic Canzone's double closing the account after Pereda and Arozarena had cashed three. Criswell took the win; twelve hits backed him. Boston's answer was the rookie Roman Anthony's second career homer and run-scoring doubles from Story and White, thin fare for a club that has now dropped two straight with its catching corps in the ward's columns above. The Puget Sound men take the series and sail for home to receive the Athletics this very evening; the Crimson Hose proceed to Baltimore, where the wounded Birds await at 7:15.

MORABITO WAITS A CAREER FOR ONE HIT AND MAKES IT A THREE-RUN DOUBLE: METROPOLITANS 10, RAYS 4

The last-place Metropolitans spent an evening battering the American's best record, and the sweetest swing belonged to a man who had never hit safely in the majors: Nick Morabito, whose seventh-inning double cleared three runners home for his first big-league hit — and who added a diving catch besides, the wires attesting to the leather as warmly as the lumber. Juan Soto struck his three-and-twentieth homer in the eighth, Brett Baty drove in three, and fourteen hits in all carried New York past a Tampa nine whose starter Jax, returned that very day from the elbow discomfort the ward had logged, was beaten in his return and charged with the loss. The Rays remain three and a half clear atop the East for all that; the Mets, at three-and-sixty wins, remain what they are — but Wednesday they were the better club by six runs, and no asterisk attaches.

TUESDAY'S FARCE IS ANSWERED WITH WEDNESDAY'S REVENGE, TWO RUNS IN THE TENTH DOING THE OFFICE: GIANTS 5, BUCS 4, IN TEN INNINGS

One evening after Pittsburgh's 13-12 carnival filled this paper's lead column, the Orange and Black returned the indignity in extra innings. Rafael Devers opened the contest with his two-and-thirtieth homer, the clubs traded the lead by increments, and in the tenth Bryce Eldridge's double and Turner Hill's sacrifice fly built the two-run margin that Nick Gonzales's answering single could only halve — the loss falling to Doval, the win to Foley, the save to Smith. The Bucs' three-game winning streak thus dies at three, and the wild-card arithmetic that had begun to whisper to them recedes to five and a half games; the set concludes at 12:35 this very afternoon, Tidwell opposing Bachar.

CEASE TAKES CLEAR TITLE TO THE STRIKEOUT CROWN, AND VLADIMIR THE YOUNGER DRIVES IN FIVE: JAYS 11, GUARDIANS 0

The corridor meeting this paper appointed came off entirely to Toronto's liking. One night after Cleveland's Williams struck out thirteen to draw level, Dylan Cease answered with six scoreless innings for his tenth victory, his four strikeouts carrying him to 221 and sole possession of the American's lead, four clear of his rival. The hitting was Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s personal property: a two-run double in the first, a three-run homer in the second, a run-scoring single in the sixth — five driven in, and the wire desks asking aloud whether the vintage article has returned. Josh Smith homered besides, and the eleven-run whitewashing carried a standings cruelty noted in the lead column: the Guardians, humiliated at home, lost not an inch of their chair, while the Jays climb into the three-way scrum at nine-and-sixty wins a game and a half behind them. The same clubs conclude the set at 1:10 this afternoon, Soriano opposing Bibee.

FIVE RUNS IN THE TWELFTH SETTLE A GAME THAT REFUSED SETTLING: TIGERS 11, NORTH STARS 6, IN TWELVE INNINGS

Detroit led by four in the middle innings, watched Minnesota claw level with three in the eighth — Royce Lewis's two-run single the equalizer — and then traded single runs in the eleventh, Max Clark doubling home the visitors' man and Keaschall answering. The twelfth broke the stalemate wholesale: Spencer Torkelson's two-run homer, his one-and-twentieth, followed by Javier Báez's three-run double, five runs in all. And the desk savors the decision's ironist: the victory went to Finnegan, the same reliever who surrendered the deluge in Tuesday's ten-run inning that these pages recorded — redemption arriving on a forty-eight-hour schedule. The Tigers thus snap a three-game slide; the North Stars, whose September ambitions this paper had begun to humor, see their own three-game streak snapped in the bargain.

DOWN FIVE RUNS BEFORE THE FIRST INNING CLOSED, THE FISH SWIM ALL THE WAY BACK: MARLINS 9, MISSOURIANS 6

Kansas City spent the game's first quarter-hour scoring five — Carter Jensen and Salvador Perez homering in a first-inning fusillade — and the next four hours surrendering the lead by degrees. Miami answered through Kyle Stowers's homer, a tying sixth built on singles and a sacrifice fly, and Heriberto Hernández's go-ahead double in the same frame; in the ninth Javier Sanoja and Jakob Marsee added solo blasts for punctuation, and the affair closed at four hours and nine minutes, Gibson winning in relief and Faucher sealing it. Jensen homered twice in the losing cause. The Fish, at one-and-seventy wins, sit two and a half games from the National's last chair with the season's arithmetic still speaking to them; the Missourians have dropped three running.

THE STREAK DIES AT FIVE-AND-TWENTY, AND THE BATS PAY THE PITCHER'S DEBTS: CREAM CITY NINE 9, NORTH SIDERS 5

For five-and-twenty consecutive starts Jacob Misiorowski had permitted three earned runs or fewer — a run of parsimony the wires certify — and on a humid Wrigley evening the ledger finally blotted: five runs in four innings, four walks, Alex Bregman's two-run homer the heaviest entry against him. Whereupon his mates paid the account in full: Jackson Chourio's one-and-twentieth homer in the second, then a three-run fourth — Turang's squeeze bunt and run-scoring singles from Vaughn and Contreras — turning a five-three deficit into the lead, with Pratt adding one in the seventh and Joey Ortiz's two-run knock in the ninth closing the books at nine runs and fourteen hits, the pitcher's blemish forgiven. Bregman drove in four of Chicago's five. At seven-and-eighty wins the Cream City nine hold the game's best record and a nine-game lead over the North Siders, whom they oblige again at 7:15 this evening, Henderson opposing Gausman — and the deposed streak-keeper retains, for consolation, the National's crowns in earned runs and strikeouts alike.

WESNESKI CARRIES ONE HIT THROUGH SEVEN, VELÁZQUEZ CASHES THE ONLY COIN: SPACE CITY MEN 2, WHITE STOCKINGS 0

The set's finale, upon which two divisions leaned as this paper observed, went to Houston on the arm of Hayden Wesneski — seven innings, one hit, five strikeouts — and a single eighth-inning stroke: Nelson Velázquez's two-run single off the reliever Newcomb, the game's entire scoring. Josh Hader sealed his two-and-twentieth save. Chicago, which had taken the set's first two games as this paper recorded, managed three hits in the finale, though the White Stockings' hold on the Central survives at three games over beaten Cleveland; the Space City men, for their part, stretch the West's margin to two full games over Texas, whose own evening the card above laments. The clubs meet again at 2:10 this afternoon, Castillo opposing Brown.

SCHLITTLER AND DETMERS DUEL THROUGH SEVEN, AND THE TENTH INNING BREAKS FOR NEW YORK AT LAST: YANKEES 6, ANAHEIM NINE 3, IN TEN INNINGS

The rubber match this paper commended to the night owls delivered its promised duel: Cam Schlittler eight innings of two hits, nine strikeouts, and not a walk — the American's earned-run leader at 2.04 confirming the title — opposite Reid Detmers's seven innings of one run, the game standing one apiece into extra innings on Vaughn Grissom's seventh-inning equalizer. The tenth resolved it wholesale: five New York runs on a procession of singles — Austin Wells cashing two, Bellinger, Grisham, and Rice one apiece — against which Moisés Ballesteros's two-run answer was ornament. Bednar took the win with three strikeouts in relief. The Yankees, at eighty wins, hold second in the East three and a half behind Tampa Bay and sail for San Diego, where Friday's opener brings the piggyback arrangement of Fried and Warren these pages have advertised.

SAGGESE AGAIN, AND AGAIN — THE TENTH INNING RESTORES THE REDBIRDS TO .500: REDBIRDS 8, ANGELENOS 6, IN TEN INNINGS

Two evenings after his two-homer night filled these columns, Thomas Saggese supplied both the sixth-inning homer that began the comeback and the tenth-inning single that won it, Joshua Báez's two-run double stretching the margin behind him. The road back was long: Freddie Freeman's three-run first off the young Mautz, Mookie Betts answering Saggese's first blow in kind, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto dominant into the seventh — whereupon the rookie Leo Bernal, whose Tuesday debut this paper toasted, struck his first major-league homer, and Alec Burleson's eighth-inning sacrifice fly, his hundred-and-first run driven in, leveled the account. O'Brien's five-and-thirtieth save closed it. St. Louis thus stands restored to level at seventy wins and seventy defeats; the Angelenos have dropped two straight with the great Ohtani's condition the graver concern, as the ward relates, and the clubs finish at 10:10 this evening, Mathews opposing Skubal.

BRITO'S FIRST HOMER CLEARS THREE RUNS, AND THE RUBBER MATCH GOES TO THE QUEEN CITY: REDS 7, FRIARS 3

The 12:40 rubber match this paper flagged went to the home nine in one violent second inning: Juan Brito, batting with two aboard, struck the first home run of his major-league life, and Héctor Rodríguez followed in the same frame with another — four runs where San Diego had led by three, the advantage never returned. JJ Bleday's two-run drive in the seventh, his two-and-twentieth, closed the account; Williamson beat Mize precisely as the probables promised. Ty France's early two-run homer and Fernando Tatis Jr.'s two hits were the visitors' portion, caught by the debutant Salas whose historic afternoon the vestibule desk records above. The defeat is costly: a second straight for the Friars, who surrender the National's last chair to Arizona by half a game — the season's cruelest denomination of coin.

The tables on the third morning of September, taken in one turning. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the East by three and a half over New York, with Boston eight and a half astern; the White Stockings keep the Central by three over Cleveland; Houston's crown in the West is two games over Texas. The wild-card row reads New York and Boston comfortable, and then the morning's best theatre: Cleveland's last chair defended by a game and a half over Texas, Toronto, and Baltimore — three clubs at identical figures of nine-and-sixty and one-and-seventy, pressed against one door with four-and-twenty days remaining, the season's final regular card falling on the seven-and-twentieth and the wild-card series opening two days after. In the National: Atlanta by four over Philadelphia; Milwaukee, owner of the game's best ledger, by nine over Chicago; Los Angeles by nine over Arizona — and the last chair now Arizona's by half a game over San Diego, with Miami two and a half back, St. Louis three and a half, and Pittsburgh's whisper fading. Tonight's card runs to nine engagements, all verified against the schedule, and the desk directs the eye to four: at 1:10 in Cleveland the wounded Guardians must answer an eleven-run insult, Soriano opposing Bibee; at 7:15 the Crimson Hose visit the wounded Birds, Bennett against Young, two limping contenders propping one another up; at 7:15 likewise the Cream City nine offer the North Siders their remedy, Henderson opposing Gausman; and at 8:05 the American's best visit Texas, McClanahan against Quantrill. The night owls are commended to Chavez Ravine at 10:10, where the Redbirds, restored to level, try the Angelenos once more. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: THE ADVERTISED DUEL OF ACES YIELDS FIVE-AND-TWENTY RUNS, AND THE LAST ONE SCORES ON A THROW GONE ASTRAY: CORSAIRS 13, GIANTS 12
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 56 · Wednesday, the Second of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE ADVERTISED DUEL OF ACES YIELDS FIVE-AND-TWENTY RUNS, AND THE LAST ONE SCORES ON A THROW GONE ASTRAY: CORSAIRS 13, GIANTS 12

Billed in these pages as the month's handsomest pitching card, Webb against Skenes becomes instead a carnival of five-and-thirty hits: Webb is excused after two innings bearing nine runs, Pittsburgh scores nine in the third without an extra-base blow among them, San Francisco claws all the way level with five in the eighth — and in the ninth Brandon Lowe's fourth hit begets the winning run on a third baseman's throw pulled wide of first

The desk begins with a confession of its own part in the evening's comedy. Yesterday's number directed the reader to Pittsburgh for as handsome a pitching card as September would offer — Logan Webb opposing Paul Skenes, an engagement for the connoisseurs — and the pastime, which reads this paper's appointments chiefly for the pleasure of mocking them, returned instead five-and-twenty runs and five-and-thirty hits. Webb was excused after two innings bearing nine hits and nine runs; Skenes did not survive the fifth, charged with five. The Giants had struck first and heavily, a five-run second built on singles by Koss and Hill and crowned by Rafael Devers's three-run blast, his one-and-thirtieth — whereupon the home third answered with nine runs assembled entirely of small coinage: singles by Oneil Cruz (twice in the frame), Davis, Horwitz, and their fellows, walks to Gonzalez and Triolo with the bases full, and not one extra-base blow in the lot. "I don't think I've seen that many singles and walks," marveled Brandon Lowe, "and to be able to put that kind of production up on the board without some sort of extra-base hit."

An eleven-to-five lead by the middle innings looked like safe harbor, and was nothing of the sort. Lowe's nine-and-twentieth homer stretched the account to twelve in the seventh, but the eighth undid nearly all of it: the reliever Sisk walked three of the four men he faced, Weaver arrived to no better fortune, and San Francisco's five-run reply ran Basabe's bases-loaded walk into Drew Cavanaugh's two-run double and the pinch-hitter Furman's two-run single — twelve runs apiece, the evening's ledger wiped clean. The accounting to that point was general on both sides: Cruz four hits and four driven in, Turner Hill four hits of his own, Devers three runs batted in, nineteen Pittsburgh hits against sixteen for the visitors.

The ninth supplied the ending such an evening deserved. Lowe led off with his fourth hit, took third on the traffic that followed, and with two out Rafael Flores Jr. bounced a grounder to Basabe — shifted by then from second base across to third — whose throw sailed past Devers at first as Lowe came home with the thirteenth run. "Eventful," ruled the manager Kelly, in the evening's finest economy of language, before crediting the third inning's democracy: "Everybody contributed in that inning to help us score nine runs." Flores took the wider view: "It's kind of what you live for. You want to play games like that." The win fell to the reliever Montgomery, the loss to Seymour, and the Corsairs have now won three running — eight-and-sixty victories against one-and-seventy defeats, five games from the National's last wild-card chair and refusing, as yet, to be shown the door. The clubs go again this evening at 6:40, Roupp opposing Jones, and the desk makes no promises whatever about the pitching.

News Around the League

THE OWNERSHIP DESK: THE ANGELS CHANGE HANDS — KROENKE OF THE RAMS AGREES TO BUY THE FRANCHISE, AND THE MORENO ERA CLOSES AT THREE-AND-TWENTY YEARS

The morning's heaviest news arrived not from any diamond but from the counting-house: Stan Kroenke, proprietor of the Los Angeles Rams and of the sprawling Kroenke Sports & Entertainment concern, has reached an agreement to purchase the Angels from Arte Moreno and the Moreno family, the transaction expected to close in the first quarter of 2027 pending the approval of the league's owners. The price was not disclosed — the gentlemen of the purse rarely volunteer such figures, though the Herald observes that no man sells a ball club these days save at a fortune of the first order. Moreno, who bought the club in 2003 and has held it three-and-twenty years, will retain a minority stake; his stewardship brought six division titles in its first dozen seasons and not one winning campaign since 2015, a ledger the faithful of Anaheim know by heart.

The testimonials were duly exchanged. "The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market," said Kroenke. "We look forward to an exciting future." Moreno pronounced KSE "the best next owner." And Mike Trout, who has spent his entire glorious career in the uniform and deserves an October more than any man living, offered the endorsement that matters most in the clubhouse: "Kroenke's got a track record of success and winning championships with his teams. I'm super excited." The club marked the occasion in the evening by losing to New York, as the card below relates — the sale closing on a nine of three-and-fifty wins against six-and-eighty defeats, with everywhere to go but down.

THE DEBUT DESK: TWO FIRST-NIGHT HOMERS IN A SINGLE EVENING CARRY THE FRESHMAN CLASS TO A RECORD FIFTEEN — MONTES THUNDERS AT FENWAY, MORALES IN THE CAPITAL

This desk, which attended Walker Jenkins daily through his first week, now finds the whole freshman class crowding its columns. Tuesday evening produced two first-game homers in two different cities, and with them a record: fifteen men have now homered in their major-league debuts this season, no year since 1900 having produced more than the thirteen of 2022. At Fenway Park, Lazaro Montes — the Mariners' summons from the September expansion, owner of eight-and-thirty minor-league homers this summer, the second-most in all the bushes — walked in his first appearance, singled home a run in his third inning, and in the fifth deposited a low slider 407 feet to center field. "I'm trying to be me, be myself," said the one-and-twenty-year-old. "I give it my 100 percent." His manager Wilson testified that "certainly that energy has been a big lift" — the fuller destruction his club visited upon Boston stands in the card below. In Washington the selfsame night, Yohandy Morales struck his own first-game homer in the third inning of the Senators' rout of Atlanta, the record-breaking fifteenth of the class.

Nor was the night's debuting done: in Los Angeles the Cardinals' Leo Bernal, their seventh-ranked prospect, announced himself with a bases-loaded, two-run single at 107.6 miles to the hour by the trackers' certificate — "Being in this clubhouse with these people, against the team that we faced... was special and the hard work paid off," said the young man, whose fuller evening the card below sings. The desk notes for the almanac that the class of 2026 has made a habit of arriving loudly: Wetherholt, Benge, Murakami, and DeLauter all homered on Opening Day itself, and the Cardinal Báez struck three in his August debut.

THE LAUREL DESK: THE SEPTEMBER CANVASS FINDS McGONIGLE AND STEWART PULLING CLEAR IN THE ROOKIE RACES

The wire desks' September polling of the Rookie of the Year question finds both races acquiring the shape of verdicts. In the American, Detroit's Kevin McGonigle commands 186 points and thirty first-place ballots of the electors, his 6.1 wins above replacement leading every rookie in either league, his .375 on-base figure and 140 hits leading the American's freshmen. Cleveland's left-hander Parker Messick (132 points) and the White Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami (124, with his nine-and-twenty homers) divide the remaining first-place sentiment. In the National, the case this paper weighed on Sunday has only hardened: Cincinnati's Sal Stewart, at one-and-thirty homers and one hundred five runs batted in — the latter figure leading all baseball, not merely the rookies — polls 173 points and four-and-twenty firsts, and the historical brief is unanswerable: every freshman to pair thirty homers with a hundred runs batted in since the award began in 1947 has taken the trophy home. The Cardinal JJ Wetherholt stands second at 140 points, though his candidacy campaigns from the invalid list, whither his wrist dispatched him on Sunday as this ward recorded; the Met pitcher Nolan McLean is third. The Herald, which does not vote, ventures only that the freshmen have rarely given the electors so little suspense and so much pleasure.

THE VESTIBULE DESK: SALAS ARRIVES IN CINCINNATI AFTER THE FIRST PITCH, AND WAITS ONE DAY MORE FOR HIS FIRST

The summons this paper's dealings desk recorded yesterday came due — after a fashion. Ethan Salas, the Padres' anointed catcher of the future, received the call of his life Monday night ("It's a cool phone call, one you dream about every single day as a kid"), then spent his first day as a big-leaguer marooned at the El Paso airport, arriving at the Cincinnati grounds only after the first pitch had been thrown. He changed into flannels bearing the No. 8, emerged into the dugout in the third inning, and worked his way down the railing shaking hands. His manager Stammen, with a one-run game and a pennant race in his charge, declined to spend the debut so cheaply — though he allowed that had the game reached extra innings, the twenty-year-old was his next man off the bench. The club envisions him for now as a third catcher and a useful left-handed bat; when he does first don the tools of ignorance in a game, he will be the youngest man to catch in the majors since Iván Rodríguez in 1991, as yesterday's number observed. The debutant himself kept the long view: "The end goal was never to make it here. It's obviously to stay." His new club's evening went less serenely — the card below has the particulars — and the vestibule may open as soon as this afternoon's 12:40 rubber match.

THE RESTORATION DESK: THE CHAMPIONS RECEIVE THREE MEN BACK IN ONE AFTERNOON — AND IN CINCINNATI, DE LA CRUZ ANSWERS THE WARD'S ALARM AT A RUN

The appointment stood and was kept: the Dodgers on Tuesday activated their catcher Will Smith from three months' exile with an inflamed disc of the neck, precisely as this paper's restoration desk appointed on Monday, and returned the reserve catcher Dalton Rushing and the pitcher Justin Wrobleski from the invalid rolls in the same stroke — three men in an afternoon, the September reinforcement arriving on schedule even if, as the card below relates, the evening's baseball declined to cooperate. Smith, for his part, doubled in his first game back, which is more than most men manage after a season's middle spent in a neck brace. And in Cincinnati the ward retires an alarm it sounded Sunday with foreboding: Elly De La Cruz, whose left quadriceps lifted him from that afternoon's game and sent this desk to its worry-drawer, was back at shortstop Tuesday and crossed the plate with the go-ahead run in the eighth inning of the Reds' 4-3 victory. The quadriceps, it appears, has been persuaded; the Herald's worry-drawer closes gladly on both cities.

The Rest of the Card

THE GAS HOUSE NINE STRIKE FIVE HOMERS AND A NUMBER NO CARDINAL CLUB EVER POSTED AT CHAVEZ RAVINE: CARDINALS 13, DODGERS 8

On the very evening the champions restored three men to the ranks, St. Louis spoiled the housewarming with the heaviest night any Cardinal club has ever spent at Dodger Stadium — thirteen runs, a figure never before reached in 337 games on those grounds. The blows came five over the fence: Ramón Urías and Thomas Saggese in succession in the second, Jordan Walker's two-run drive in the fourth — 409 feet at 109.3 miles to the hour, and a curiosity for the cabinet: his five-and-fiftieth career homer struck off his five-and-fiftieth different pitcher, the second-longest such run since 1900 behind Adames's seven-and-fifty — Saggese again in the fifth, and the young Joshua Báez in the seventh. Saggese's pair, struck hard by his boyhood California home with his father in the stands, made the first two-homer night of his major-league life and doubled his career count to four in a single evening. The rookie Bernal's 107.6-mile debut single crowned a five-run third, as the debut desk relates; McGreevy pitched to the victory. The champions' account was chiefly Mookie Betts, two doubles and four driven in, with Smith's return-day double noted in the restoration desk above. The Boys in Blue thus surrender a half-game of their bye cushion nowhere — idle Atlanta lost too, as the card below records — but the West's lead over San Diego is nine and a half, and the rematch comes at 10:10 this evening with Yamamoto restored to the hill.

THREE MEN CONVERGE UPON ONE POP FLY AND ALL RISE; MILWAUKEE RISES LIKEWISE, FROM THREE DOWN TO A ROUT: BREW CREW 9, CUBS 4

The Wrigley argument's second evening reversed the first with interest. Chicago banked three fourth-inning runs — Taylor's two-run double the freight, Monday's unfortunate emergency pitcher Andrew Vaughn contributing to the rally's setup from first base — and Milwaukee answered with nine unanswered until a late Cubs run: Pratt's run-scoring single in the fifth, then a four-run sixth in which Vaughn, restored to his proper trade, doubled home the tying run and Christian Yelich struck the go-ahead two-run homer, his tenth. William Contreras doubled twice more in the seventh, Frelick singled home another, and Joey Ortiz closed the accounts with a two-run drive in the eighth — the Brew Crew's six-and-thirtieth comeback victory of the season, Senzatela collecting the decision in relief. The evening's held breath came in the sixth, when Chourio, Pratt, and Ortiz converged at full gallop upon Busch's pop fly to shallow left and went down in a tangle as the ball fell for a double; the trainers attended all three, and all three stayed in the game. "I think everyone wanted it, which is a good thing," said Ortiz. The arithmetic this paper set out Monday now runs the other way: the Central gap is back to eight games, Milwaukee holds the season's series five games to three with five meetings left inside eight days, and tonight the visitors send Misiorowski — fourteen victories, an earned-run figure of 1.73, and the National's strikeout lead — against Peterson at 7:40.

HARPER REACHES FIVE TIMES, LUZARDO CARRIES THE SEVENTH, AND THE SIXTH STRAIGHT BUYS SOLE TITLE TO THE TOP CHAIR: PHILLIES 7, SONORAN NINE 1

The Brotherly Love nine made it six victories running by the simplest of formulas: Bryce Harper refused to be retired — four hits and a walk, five times aboard, his on-base streak now four-and-thirty games — and Jesús Luzardo pitched into the seventh bearing a single run, his ledger now thirteen victories against five. Turner's run-scoring double and a first-inning double play cashed two early; Bohm singled home Harper in the fifth; and the late innings added four by instalments, Crawford and Harper singling home runs around sacrifice flies from Schwarber and Stott. Arizona's whole account was the young Lawlar's fourth homer, and the defeat — a fourth straight — is costly coin: the Snakes of Monday's number slip a half-game from the National's last chair. Philadelphia, meanwhile, banks the prize this surge has been buying toward: sole possession of the wild-card's top chair at nine-and-seventy wins, one clear of Chicago, with the Eastern gap to Atlanta down to three. The clubs conclude in the desert at 3:40 this afternoon, Painter opposing Clarke.

PERALTA MEETS HIS FORMER EMPLOYERS AND SUBMITS THE EVIDENCE OF HIS RECOVERY: TAMPA MEN 6, METS 2

Freddy Peralta, shipped from New York to Tampa Bay at the deadline for three prospects after a season of five-and-nine and an earned-run figure near five, faced the Mets for the first time since the transaction and pitched as if settling the account line by line: six innings, three hits, one run, not a walk, seven strikeouts. "I have my confidence back," said the right-hander, whose two starts as a Ray are now two victories. "I think that's a more important thing for a pitcher, when you trust in your stuff again." His catcher Yandy Díaz furnished the offense besides the testimony — a homer, a double, and two runs driven in — with Vilade, Fortes, and Walls filling out a thirteen-hit evening. Lindor's leadoff homer and a bases-loaded walk were the whole of the visitors' account. The Tampa men, at three-and-eighty wins, keep the American's best ledger and a four-and-a-half-game lead in the East; the rubber match goes at 6:40 this evening under the dome.

TATIS STRIKES TWO, AND IT BUYS NOTHING — THE RED STOCKINGS TAKE THE EIGHTH AND THE GAME: REDS 4, PADRES 3

Fernando Tatis Jr. gave San Diego a solo homer in the fifth and another in the ninth, his eighteenth and nineteenth, and departed Cincinnati beaten anyway. The decisive eighth belonged to the home nine: Trevino's single cashed De La Cruz with the go-ahead run — the restoration desk above has the gladder meaning of that sentence — and Brito's sacrifice fly added the insurance that Tatis's second blast could only trim. The reliever Burke took the decision, Pagán sealed his twentieth save, and the loss fell to Morejon, whose two-thirds of an inning in the eighth unraveled a game his club led nowhere but never trailed until it mattered. The defeat, set beside Arizona's below, leaves the Padres' hold on the National's last chair at half a game — with the new arrival Salas watching from the dugout rail, as the vestibule desk relates — and this afternoon's 12:40 rubber match, Mize opposing Williamson, decides the set.

WILLIAMS STRIKES OUT THIRTEEN FOR A CAREER HIGH, AND THREE TWO-RUN BLASTS DO THE REST: LAKE ERIE MEN 6, MAPLE LEAF NINE 1

Gavin Williams opened the set that bears most directly upon the American's last chair by striking out thirteen Torontos across seven innings — the highest count of his life, two hits and an unearned run the only blemishes — and his mates supplied the scoring in matched pairs: two-run homers from the catcher Bailey in the fifth, the young Genao in the seventh, and Angel Martínez in the eighth — six runs in three identical strokes, Martínez crossing the plate three times himself. Fourteen strikeouts in all for the home staff; the visitors' run scored on a wild pitch. Cleveland has now won eight of ten, and the victory holds the last wild-card chair by a game and a half over Texas and Baltimore alike. The set continues at 6:40 this evening with a delicacy for the connoisseur: Cease, who shares the American's strikeout lead at 217 with the very Williams who just cleared his own bar, takes the hill for Toronto against Cantillo — the co-leaders in the same yard on consecutive nights.

FIVE RUNS IN THE SECOND, A DEBUT OF THUNDER, AND THE SKID IS SNAPPED AT FIVE: MARINERS 9, FENWAY MEN 6

Seattle, five times beaten running as yesterday's number tallied, spent one Fenway second inning ending the argument: five runs, Crawford's sacrifice fly and Rodden's single opening the ledger before Randy Arozarena's three-run homer, his two-and-twentieth, closed it. Canzone had led off the game with a homer, Raleigh doubled home another, and the debutant Montes — walked, singled, and homered, as the debut desk sings above — closed the scoring at nine. Bryan Woo took his tenth victory. Boston's reply came in instalments too late: Gasper, whose overnight arrival these pages recorded Tuesday, homered for a second consecutive day, White doubled home two, and Jones's two-run drive in the ninth dressed the final account. The rookie Paez bore the loss. The Fenway men, still four and a half clear in the wild-card row, get the rubber match at 4:10 this afternoon; the Seattle nine sail on with their first victory of September and a young man who looks like a reason to watch it.

TEN RUNS IN THE SIXTH INNING ALONE, AND THE BENGALS ARE BURIED WHOLESALE: TWIN CITIES NINE 15, TIGERS 2

Minnesota's sixth inning produced more runs than most clubs manage in an evening: ten of them, opened by Royce Lewis's three-run homer and sustained through Keaschall's single, Culpepper's double, and a procession the Detroit bullpen could not staunch — Finnegan facing six men and retiring one. The fuller ledger reads fifteen runs on thirteen hits: Clemens homered in the first, Jeffers added a homer and a triple among three driven in, Lewis and Culpepper three runs batted in apiece, and the rookie Jenkins, hitless on the night, scored twice anyway. Prielipp carried five scoreless innings in relief for the victory; Melton, whose earned-run figure had been among the American's best, bore seven runs and the loss. Three straight now for the Twin Cities nine, whose September appetite this paper remarked yesterday — the last chair sits three and a half games distant, improbable but no longer unmentionable — while the Motor City men have lost three running and eight of ten, and must send Anderson against Kremer on the same grounds at 7:40 tonight.

FOUR IN THE SECOND, A DEBUT BLAST IN THE THIRD, AND ATLANTA DROPS A SECOND STRAIGHT IN THE CAPITAL: SENATORS 9, BRAVES 5

Washington's second inning broke the game open — CJ Abrams's two-run single and Brady House's two-run double the heavy freight — and the rookie Morales opened the third with the first-game homer the debut desk celebrates above. House added a sacrifice fly among his three driven in, Young and Chaparro singled home late runs, and when Atlanta's eighth closed to within three on a wild pitch and Michael Harris II's two-run homer, the Senators answered at once and shut the door. The loss went to Smith-Shawver, four innings and five runs in a September audition that gave the wire desks fresh cause to wonder whether he figures in Atlanta's October arrangements; the win went to the reliever Simpson, three perfect innings with three strikeouts. Albies homered besides for the visitors. The Tomahawk men have now dropped two straight on the heels of their seven-game streak, and the cost is counted in two ledgers: the East's lead over surging Philadelphia is down to three, and the second bye belongs this morning to Los Angeles by half a game. The clubs meet again at 1:05 this very afternoon, Holmes opposing Lord.

SIX STINTS WITH THE CLUB THIS SEASON, AND AT LAST A NIGHT TO KEEP: FISH 6, ROYALS 3

Graham Pauley has been summoned to Miami and returned to the minors so often this summer — six separate engagements with the big club, by the wires' count — that the man might reasonably keep his bags packed by the clubhouse door. Tuesday he unpacked: a two-run homer in the second, a two-run triple in the seventh, and a run scored on Sanoja's single directly after, four driven in altogether on the finest night of his major-league life. Stowers added a solo blast, his seventeenth, and Phillips pitched five innings of one hit for the victory while Kansas City's account waited until the eighth — Jensen's double and Witt's sacrifice fly, with Loftin's ninth-inning homer the coda. The Fish, three games from the National's last chair, have designs on the same arithmetic as half the league; the Royal blues, whose August surge these pages chronicled at length, have now dropped three of four, and the clubs go again at 7:40 this evening.

NIMMO COLLECTS FOUR HITS AND FIVE RUNS BATTED IN, AND THE WEST'S GAP SHRINKS TO ONE: LONE STAR NINE 8, MACKMEN 5

Brandon Nimmo spent the evening driving in Texas runs by every legal means short of the homer: a run-scoring double in the first, singles cashing runs in the third, fifth, and sixth — four hits, five driven in, and the Arlington grandstand chanting a man's name in September for reasons beyond nostalgia. Seager doubled twice and scored ahead of him repeatedly, sacrifice flies from O'Hoppe and Seager fattened the sixth, and Gore pitched into the sixth for his eighth victory, Latz recording the final two outs by strikeout for his eight-and-twentieth save. The Mackmen's late push — McNeil's two-run homer in the ninth the chief of it — arrived too late by three innings. Three straight now for the Lone Star nine, whose home ledger of nine-and-thirty wins against nine-and-twenty defeats keeps fueling the push: they stand this morning one game from Houston's crown — the leaders having lost, as the card below relates — and a game and a half from the wild-card row. The same clubs meet at 2:35 this afternoon.

SEAN BURKE ALLOWS ONE HIT INTO THE SIXTH, AND THE MEETING OF LEADERS TILTS SOUTH SIDE: WHITE SOX 5, ASTROS 1

The September collision of division leaders now reads two games to none for Chicago: Sean Burke carried a single hit into the sixth inning — five and two-thirds scoreless in all, six strikeouts against four walks he stranded methodically — and Houston finished the evening with three hits entire. The scoring waited for the fifth, when Benintendi singled home the first run and Colson Montgomery doubled home two more; Grichuk's two-run double in the seventh supplied the margin, and Paredes's eighteenth homer in the eighth spoiled only the shutout. The South Siders hold the Central by three over Cleveland, which matched them win for win; the Houston nine's crown in the West, two games wide on Monday, is down to a single game over Texas — and the set concludes at 8:10 this evening, Martin opposing Wesneski, with the standings of two divisions leaning on the result.

RUMFIELD BREAKS THE TIE, THE HOME SKID DIES AT TEN, AND BALTIMORE'S STAY AT .500 LASTS EXACTLY ONE DAY: MILE HIGH NINE 4, ORIOLES 2

The Coloradans had lost ten consecutive games at their own yard — the longest home skid in all the franchise's annals — and chose the visit of a surging club to end it. Amador's homer and McCarthy's run-scoring single built an early two; Baltimore clawed level by increments, Narváez scoring on a double play in the third and Jackson Holliday — three hits on the night — tying the account with his seventh homer in the seventh; whereupon TJ Rumfield answered in the home half with a two-run drive to right-center, his fourteenth, and the thing was done. Hill took his first victory of the season, Romano the save. For the Baltimores the toll is precise and a little cruel: level at .500 on Monday for the first time since April, they stand a game under this morning, a game and a half from Cleveland's chair — the pursuit, as this paper said yesterday, general, but the quarry now a step farther off. The set concludes at 3:10 this afternoon in the mountain air.

TWO HOMERS BEFORE THE FIRST OUT OF THE EVENING, AND THE SOLD CLUB IS BEATEN BESIDES: BRONX BOMBERS 7, ANGELS 3

On the day the franchise changed hands — the ownership desk above has the particulars — the Angels' evening began with Spencer Jones and Jazz Chisholm Jr. striking back-to-back homers before the first inning was a batter old, and improved little thereafter. Jones finished with three driven in and two stolen bases, Chisholm three hits, and Bellinger three hits of his own; Gerrit Cole battled into the sixth bearing eight hits but only three runs for his eighth victory, and the late innings added on through Grisham's single, Goldschmidt's sacrifice fly, and Jones's ninth-inning knock. Moore's two-run triple had briefly made a game of it. New York, four and a half behind Tampa Bay with the top wild-card chair eight and a half games deep in its pocket, sends Schlittler — the American's earned-run leader at 2.09 — into tonight's 9:38 rubber match against Detmers; and the rotation's plans run further ahead: the club intends to pair the restored Fried with Warren in piggyback fashion for Friday's opener at San Diego, the captain's own return hovering over the homestand beyond, as this ward has chronicled.

The tables at midweek, taken in one turning. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the East by four and a half over New York, with Boston eight and a half astern; the White Sox keep the Central by three over Cleveland; and the West is suddenly a knife-fight — Houston by a single game over Texas, the leaders beaten two straight on the South Side's account while the Lone Star men won their third running. The wild-card row reads New York, Boston, and Cleveland's last chair by a game and a half over Texas and Baltimore alike, with Toronto two and a half back. In the National: Atlanta's lead in the East is pared to three over Philadelphia, whose six straight have bought sole title to the wild-card's top chair, one clear of Chicago; Milwaukee's Central lead is restored to eight; Los Angeles holds the West by nine and a half — and the second bye is the champions' by half a game over Atlanta, both clubs having lost Tuesday. The last chair reads San Diego by half a game over Arizona, with Miami three back, St. Louis four, and Pittsburgh five and coming loudly, as the lead column attests. Tonight's card runs to fifteen engagements, all verified against the schedule, and the desk directs the reader's eye to four: at 12:40 in Cincinnati the rubber match may open the vestibule for young Salas, Mize opposing Williamson; at 6:40 in Cleveland the strikeout co-leaders pass in the corridor, Cease and his 217 taking the hill one night after Williams's thirteen; at 7:40 the Wrigley argument's third chapter sends Misiorowski and his 1.73 against Peterson; and at 8:10 in Houston two divisions lean on the finale of the leaders' set. The 9:38 rubber in Anaheim, Schlittler opposing Detmers, is commended to the night owls. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~
